bars|Agora Meyhanesi 1890.name: Agora Meyhanesi 1890
bars|Agora Meyhanesi 1890.teaser: A Greek captain's tavern in Balat — still open, its community long gone.
bars|Agora Meyhanesi 1890.body: Asteri Dulidis, a Greek sea captain, opened it in 1890; his son Stelyo and then his grandson Hristo Dulidis ran it after him, three generations of one family on one street. The barrel tables are the original format — wine drawn straight off a cask — which is what a meyhane was before anyone made it picturesque. Restored in 2013 by the architect Hakan Kıran, trading seven days. The sign, the family name and the neighbourhood still agree with each other. Balat, Fatih · open daily, built for long dinners

bars|The rakı sofrası.name: The rakı sofrası
bars|The rakı sofrası.teaser: Not a drink with dinner — a table that paces food across an evening.
bars|The rakı sofrası.body: Under the Turkish Food Codex, rakı is suma — grape or raisin distillate — redistilled with Pimpinella anisum in traditional copper pot stills of no more than 5,000 litres, bottled at 40 per cent minimum. Water turns it white: aslan sütü , lion's milk. The order is fixed. Cold mezes first and held a long time, then hot, then the fish. You drink at the speed of the table and never without food. Ordering rakı and eating fast is the visitor's giveaway. Any meyhane · Thursday is the night

bars|Lokanta Stambouli.name: Lokanta Stambouli
bars|Lokanta Stambouli.teaser: A Rum meyhane reopening in Pera in 2026 is not a neutral act.
bars|Lokanta Stambouli.body: Perviz Resuli has opened it on the first floor of the old Union Française building inside Minoa Pera — a deliberately plain meyhane card of cold mezes, hot mezes and the day's fish, and a room built for talking rather than for music. It works the Turkish and the Rum (Ottoman Greek) traditions together instead of choosing. Read against the 1942 wealth tax, the 1955 pogrom and the 1964 expulsions, it is the most loaded opening in the city. It opened in the first week of August 2026, so go knowing there is no track record behind it yet. Meşrutiyet Cad. 99, Asmalımescit, Beyoğlu

bars|Çiçek Pasajı.name: Çiçek Pasajı
bars|Çiçek Pasajı.teaser: The prettiest arcade on İstiklal, and the clearest map of what was taken.
bars|Çiçek Pasajı.body: Built in 1876 as the Cité de Péra by the Greek banker Hristaki Zoğrafos, on ground cleared by the 1870 Pera fire that destroyed the Naum Theatre — a Second Empire arcade of European shops and apartments. As Pera declined the shops became rough meyhanes: beer barrels rolled onto the pavement, marble slabs laid across them. It was restored in 1988, and again since. The building came back. The clientele did not. İstiklal Cad., Beyoğlu · walk it, then eat elsewhere

bars|WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas.group: Natural wine and the caves à manger
bars|WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas.name: WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas
bars|WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas.teaser: Every one of 500-plus labels open by the glass. Nowhere else does this.
bars|WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas.body: Moda, and the single most useful room in Istanbul for anyone who thinks Turkish wine means a hotel Cabernet. The house carries labels from 143 Turkish wineries and, as of July 2026, ninety endemic grape varieties — and serves the entire list by the glass, which is the whole point: you can taste eight native grapes in one evening instead of gambling a bottle on one. Tapas alongside, built to pair rather than to fill. Start here and the rest of the guide reads differently. Ferit Tek Sok. 60/B, Moda, Kadıköy · 16:00–00:00, weekends from 14:00

bars|Bağ Pera.group: Natural wine and the caves à manger
bars|Bağ Pera.name: Bağ Pera
bars|Bağ Pera.teaser: Pera's warm room for small Turkish producers, with the tasting bench upstairs.
bars|Bağ Pera.body: On İstiklal at the Asmalımescit end, pouring from around eighty-five Turkish growers against cheese, charcuterie and small hot plates sized for a glass rather than a bottle. The upstairs room runs tastings and workshops with working oenologists, frequently on boutique estates that never reach a restaurant list — which makes it the cheapest place in the city to learn the map before you start spending on it. Lunch Monday to Saturday, dinner every night. İstiklal Cad. 186, Asmalımescit, Beyoğlu · lunch Mon–Sat 12:00–14:45, dinner from 17:30

bars|Lips Wine Bar.group: Natural wine and the caves à manger
bars|Lips Wine Bar.name: Lips Wine Bar
bars|Lips Wine Bar.teaser: Nişantaşı's low-lit natural-wine room, small plates, and a hard Sunday shutter.
bars|Lips Wine Bar.body: One of the two openings that visibly thickened the natural-wine layer this year, tucked into an apartment building on a Teşvikiye side street: a short chef-driven small-plates list against low-intervention pours, and lighting dim enough to hold a table for three hours. Monday to Saturday, five in the afternoon until one in the morning. It is closed on Sundays without exception — the night visitors most often try it, and the reason to check the day before you cross town. Hacı Emin Efendi Sok., Nişantaşı Apt 24C, Teşvikiye, Şişli · Mon–Sat 17:00–01:00

bars|Öküzgözü & Boğazkere.name: Öküzgözü & Boğazkere
bars|Öküzgözü & Boğazkere.teaser: The bull's eye and the throat-scraper — Turkey's great red pairing, rarely poured apart.
bars|Öküzgözü & Boğazkere.body: Öküzgözü, 'bull's eye', comes from the villages around Elazığ and Malatya: violets, red and black plum, soft ripe tannin, medium-bodied and generous, and capable of oak without collapsing. Boğazkere grows down the Tigris from Diyarbakır and is its opposite — dense, structural, aggressively tannic, the name meaning roughly 'throat-scraper'. Blended, the first sands down the second, and that blend is what Turkey exports as its own idea. Order each on its own once, to hear what it was actually contributing. Elazığ, Malatya and Diyarbakır

bars|Kalecik Karası.name: Kalecik Karası
bars|Kalecik Karası.teaser: The Anatolian red that drinks like Gamay, and was nearly lost.
bars|Kalecik Karası.body: From Kalecik, north-east of Ankara on the Kızılırmak. Pale to medium in colour, red cherry and strawberry, low to moderate tannin — and Turkish drinkers reach almost automatically for Gamay or Pinot Noir to describe it, which tells you exactly what it is for. This is the bottle when the table is eating mezes rather than grilled meat. Serve it cool. In a country whose reputation abroad rests on tannin, it is the standing argument for the other direction. Kalecik, Ankara province

bars|Narince & Emir.name: Narince & Emir
bars|Narince & Emir.teaser: One means 'delicately'; the other grows on Cappadocian volcanic rock.
bars|Narince & Emir.body: Narince is Tokat's grape and its name means 'delicately' — aromatic, medium to full-bodied, with a texture that carries oak without losing the fruit. Emir comes off the volcanic soils of Cappadocia: high acid, mineral and savoury, sharper and more austere than Narince, and the one with real ageing capacity. Between them they cover the entire Turkish white argument, and both are absurdly cheap set against any European equivalent. Emir with fish and raw things, Narince with anything out of a wood oven. Tokat and Cappadocia

bars|Papazkarası & Çalkarası.name: Papazkarası & Çalkarası
bars|Papazkarası & Çalkarası.teaser: The two that make the country's best rosés, from opposite ends of it.
bars|Papazkarası & Çalkarası.body: Papazkarası — 'priest's black' — is Thracian, thick-skinned, high in acid and modest in tannin, now vinified as a varietal red, as blanc de noirs and as traditional-method sparkling. Çalkarası comes from the Çal district of Denizli in the inland Aegean and reaches its best as rosé: pale, dry, sharply acidic, tart cherry and pomegranate where a Provençal wine would give melon. Both are summer bottles, both are improving fast, and both are still priced as curiosities rather than as serious wine. Thrace and Denizli

bars|Arkaoda.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
bars|Arkaoda.name: Arkaoda
bars|Arkaoda.teaser: Kadıköy's anchor since 1999, and the only one with a Berlin offshoot.
bars|Arkaoda.body: Opened on Kadife Sokak in 1999 and functionally a collective rather than a bar: selectors move between Turkish psych, jazz and electronic across a night, there is a garden, and the booking leans towards independent artists nobody is paying to put on. Its Neukölln offshoot runs on the same principle, which makes this the rare Istanbul room that exported rather than imported. Open from midday to two, which means you can start an evening here and never leave. Kadife Sok. 18/1, Caferağa, Kadıköy · 12:00–02:00

bars|Karga.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
bars|Karga.name: Karga
bars|Karga.teaser: Five floors of an old wooden house, and thirty years of the Kadıköy alternative scene inside it.
bars|Karga.body: Trading since 1996 in a five-storey wooden house on Kadife Sokak, with KargART — concerts, screenings, exhibitions — on the top two floors and vinyl sessions in the small rooms below. It is the building the Kadıköy alternative scene grew up inside. The programme turns over constantly and lives on the venue's Instagram rather than on its website, which is a blank splash page: check the feed for what is on the night you go. Kadife Sok. 16, Caferağa, Kadıköy · programme on Instagram

bars|Nayah.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
bars|Nayah.name: Nayah
bars|Nayah.teaser: The only terrace in Turkey given over entirely to reggae, dub and dancehall.
bars|Nayah.body: Kırtasiyeci Sokak in Kadıköy, running fifteen years and more, and narrow in the best possible way — it does one thing. Roots reggae, dub and dancehall on sound-system logic rather than DJ-set logic, live bands most weekends, and a dancefloor on the top level with the neighbourhood spread out beneath it. If the listening bars are about sitting still and hearing detail, this is the same obsession with sound pushed in the opposite direction. Kırtasiyeci Sok. 30/A, Kadıköy

bars|June.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
bars|June.name: June
bars|June.teaser: A neighbourhood bar that listens first and dances later, on a Teşvikiye street.
bars|June.body: Ahmet Fetgeri Sokak, and one of the two rooms that pulled the listening format across onto the European side this year. Dim, minimal, vinyl-led, with a proper short kitchen list instead of the usual bar snacks — the early evening is built to be heard, and the tempo climbs until people are dancing between the tables. Not a temple, and it does not want to be: the sound is serious, the room is not, and that combination is the whole appeal. Ahmet Fetgeri Sok. 31, Teşvikiye, Şişli

bars|Dama.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
bars|Dama.name: Dama
bars|Dama.teaser: Filter coffee by day, vinyl through serious speakers once the light goes.
bars|Dama.body: Şakayık Sokak in Teşvikiye, and its own line is 'café by day, hi-fi by night'. Mornings are filter coffee, breakfast and laptops on a quiet side street; the evening hands the room to vinyl through a system somebody clearly spent real money on, with an open kitchen, ceramic surfaces and shelves of records. Short seasonal cocktail list, small plates. The cleanest single example of the format Istanbul has adopted faster than anywhere else. Şakayık Sok. 19, Teşvikiye, Şişli

bars|Frankhan.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
bars|Frankhan.name: Frankhan
bars|Frankhan.teaser: A Karaköy han, a main floor for dancing, and a second, much smaller room behind it.
bars|Frankhan.body: Opened in 2023 by the Selectist team inside a Karaköy han, running house, electro and live electronic on the main floor. Behind it sits the Sound Room, a far smaller space held within the original walls of the han. Check which of the two rooms is open on the night; they do not always run together. Karaköy, Beyoğlu

bars|FLUX.name: FLUX
bars|FLUX.teaser: Funktion-One in Maslak, and the two nights are deliberately not the same night.
bars|FLUX.body: An RX Istanbul project in a modular room that scales from fifty to five hundred indoors plus a two-hundred-capacity terrace, on Funktion-One. The programming split is explicit and worth planning around: Fridays run house , groove-led and rhythmic; Saturdays go techno , deeper and harder. The opening season, autumn 2025, carried Ben Klock, Anja Schneider, Cormac, Setaoc Mass and Stef Mendesidis; 2026 has run to Rødhåd, Regal, Tommy Four Seven, Adriana Lopez and FJAAK. This is the serious room, and it is a long way north — budget for the taxi. Maslak, Sarıyer · late

bars|Şahika.name: Şahika
bars|Şahika.teaser: Multi-level in Beyoğlu, roof terrace on top, the odd end of the programming.
bars|Şahika.body: Several floors climbing to a rooftop terrace, and the place to go when four-to-the-floor is not what you want: jungle and footwork alongside techno and house, local selectors with European guests, and exhibitions, talks and performances sharing the same building. Queer-friendly by reputation and in practice, which in this city is a specific and not automatic thing to be. Start on the roof at the end of the light and work downwards as it gets louder. Beyoğlu

bars|NOH Radio Bar / NOH Extended.name: NOH Radio Bar / NOH Extended
bars|NOH Radio Bar / NOH Extended.teaser: So small the music goes out into the street, plus a late annexe.
bars|NOH Radio Bar / NOH Extended.body: Two rooms and one idea. The Radio Bar in Firuzağa is compact enough that the sound spills onto the pavement and the crowd stands outside with it — electronic, house, trance, visiting DJs, no pretence at a door policy. NOH Extended on Tosbağa Sokak is the late half: multi-level, exhibition space upstairs, club underneath, and the particular mix of underground scene, art crowd and record obsessives that Beyoğlu still assembles better than anywhere across the water. Firuzağa and Tosbağa Sok. 14/A, Tomtom, Beyoğlu

bars|Suma Han.name: Suma Han
bars|Suma Han.teaser: A Greek-built rakı distillery, now an artists' building with a club inside.
bars|Suma Han.body: Built in 1923 by the Greek architect Simotas and worked as a rakı distillation plant. Bought in 2003, restored, and reopened in 2009 as offices, artist studios, residences and common rooms with a club floor and genuine acoustics folded in — two stages, techno and psy-trance, plus exhibitions and talks. That the city's clearest case of artists building their own infrastructure sits inside a Greek-built rakı works is not a coincidence this guide is going to let pass. Beyoğlu

bars|POPSTEL — Stay Local.name: POPSTEL — Stay Local
bars|POPSTEL — Stay Local.teaser: The night that ignores techno entirely: Y2K rap, UK garage, dark disco.
bars|POPSTEL — Stay Local.body: Not a club so much as a series, run out of a hostel bar on Tomtom Sokak in Galatasaray, and the necessary correction to a city that can feel as though it only plays four-to-the-floor. Stay Local works Y2K hip-hop, UK garage and dark disco to a young local crowd rather than an imported-headliner one, which is the entire premise of the name. Check the dates: the room is only worth the walk when the series is actually on. Tomtom, Galatasaray, Beyoğlu · check dates before going

rooftops|The Bank Roof Bar.group: Looking back at the old city
rooftops|The Bank Roof Bar.name: The Bank Roof Bar
rooftops|The Bank Roof Bar.teaser: A drink on the roof of the street that financed the Ottoman Empire.
rooftops|The Bank Roof Bar.body: Bankalar Caddesi — Voyvoda Caddesi on the older maps — was the financial centre of the late Ottoman Empire, and the houses that built it were largely Galata's Jewish, Greek and Armenian banking families; the Camondos cut their baroque staircase down the hill to it in the nineteenth century. The banks left for Levent in the 1990s. The hotel took one of their buildings at No. 5, and the terrace looks across the Golden Horn to Hagia Sophia, Topkapı and the Blue Mosque. Azapkapı, Bankalar Cd. No:5, Karaköy, Beyoğlu · daily, midday until late

rooftops|Roof106.group: Looking back at the old city
rooftops|Roof106.name: Roof106
rooftops|Roof106.teaser: Named after its own front door: Meşrutiyet Caddesi number 106.
rooftops|Roof106.body: The name is the street number. Meşrutiyet Caddesi is the Pera spine — the Pera Palace, the old consulates and The Marmara Pera all stand on it — so two of the city's roofs sit a few hundred metres apart on the same pavement at very different money. From the top of the Galata Times Hotel the line of sight runs over the Golden Horn to the peninsula, with the tower close on the left. Confirm the day as well as the hour: it closes on Tuesdays. Evliya Çelebi Mah., Meşrutiyet Cad. No:106, Beyoğlu · closed Tuesdays

rooftops|Mikla Bar.group: Looking back at the old city
rooftops|Mikla Bar.name: Mikla Bar
rooftops|Mikla Bar.teaser: The starred kitchen is downstairs; the terrace will pour you a drink without it.
rooftops|Mikla Bar.body: Mehmet Gürs's restaurant holds a MICHELIN star and occupies the top two floors of The Marmara Pera, but the bar is a separate proposition. It opens at 18:00 and runs to 02:00, has an outdoor terrace and a pool, and does not require the tasting menu — you can sit at it for the price of a cocktail. It is the highest roof on Meşrutiyet Caddesi, which is most of what you are paying for. The Marmara Pera, Meşrutiyet Cad., Beyoğlu · bar 18:00–02:00 · around TL 700–850 a cocktail

rooftops|Roof Mezzepotamia.group: The other shore, and the strait
rooftops|Roof Mezzepotamia.name: Roof Mezzepotamia
rooftops|Roof Mezzepotamia.teaser: The one every English guide puts on the wrong shore.
rooftops|Roof Mezzepotamia.body: It is in Sirkeci, on the historic peninsula, on the terrace of the Orient Occident Hotel — not Karaköy, where a run of English-language listings puts it. The difference is the whole point: from here you look back at Galata instead of out from it, across 270 degrees of the Bosphorus, the Golden Horn and the tower. The name folds mezze into Mesopotamia, and the kitchen runs the seven regions of Turkey. Sirkeci Station, terminus of the Orient Express from 1890, is a few doors away. Orient Occident Hotel, Hobyar Mah., Aşirefendi Cad. No:11, Sirkeci, Fatih · book for sunset · around TL 750–900 a cocktail

rooftops|Sky Karaköy.group: The other shore, and the strait
rooftops|Sky Karaköy.name: Sky Karaköy
rooftops|Sky Karaköy.teaser: Ninth floor, the strait wide open — when it is actually open.
rooftops|Sky Karaköy.body: Ninth floor of the JW Marriott İstanbul Bosphorus, above Karaköy and close enough to Galataport that the cruise ships become part of the view. Stated hours are 17:00 to 01:00 daily. The caveat is not invented: Marriott's own listing for the bar has carried a Seasonally Closed label, which is a hotel group's way of saying the roof shuts when the weather turns. Telephone the hotel before you build an evening around it. 9th floor, JW Marriott İstanbul Bosphorus, Karaköy · 17:00–01:00 · confirm it is in season

rooftops|Manifest Roof.name: Manifest Roof
rooftops|Manifest Roof.teaser: The Galata roof that does not shut when the weather turns.
rooftops|Manifest Roof.body: A short walk from the Galata Tower on Şimşir Sokak, and the only roof here that stays open through winter: a glass ceiling holds the Golden Horn in view through rain and cold, when most Galata terraces simply close. The kitchen runs a long Mediterranean and Turkish list — around sixty dishes — rather than a bar menu, so treat it as a dinner room that happens to be on a roof. Its own pages disagree about the hours; confirm when you book. Bereketzade Mah., Şimşir Sok. No:20, Beyoğlu · dinner from around 18:00 · confirm hours

rooftops|Hood.name: Hood
rooftops|Hood.teaser: The Asian side's roof, and the only one that sees everything at once.
rooftops|Hood.body: Twelve floors above Moda on the Kadıköy shore, which puts the European skyline on the far side of the water rather than underneath you: the old-city peninsula, the mouth of the Bosphorus and the Princes' Islands out in the Marmara, in one sweep. Service runs 15:00 to 23:00 and the dress code is smart casual. Getting there is a ferry crossing at dusk, which is arguably the better half of the evening. Caferağa Mah., Albay Faik Sözdener Cd. No:31, Kat 12, Kadıköy · 15:00–23:00

rooftops|What a drink costs up there.name: What a drink costs up there
rooftops|What a drink costs up there.teaser: You are buying the sightline. The drink is incidental.
rooftops|What a drink costs up there.body: Budget roughly 600 to 900 TL for a cocktail at a mainstream hotel rooftop in 2026. The marquee addresses sit above that band — current listings for the best-known Karaköy and Pera terraces run 1,000 to 1,200 TL a cocktail, The Bank Roof Bar among them. The gap between the two bands is the view, not the liquor. 2026 prices, and they move with the lira — treat them as an order of magnitude, not a quote

rooftops|The hour.name: The hour
rooftops|The hour.teaser: Turkey never puts its clocks back, so the light lasts absurdly late.
rooftops|The hour.body: Turkey abolished daylight saving on 7 September 2016 and has stayed on UTC+3 ever since, an hour ahead of its own longitude. The effect on a roof is direct: mid-August sunset falls around 20:05, with the golden hour from about 19:25 and blue light holding to about 20:35. By midwinter the same moment arrives just before 17:40. Arrive at least forty-five minutes early if you want a table on the rail. Mid-August sunset around 20:05 · winter solstice sunset 17:40

rooftops|The season.name: The season
rooftops|The season.teaser: Half these roofs simply are not there in winter.
rooftops|The season.body: An Istanbul rooftop is a summer business. Terraces glass themselves in, cut their hours or close outright from about November, and the listings do not always keep up — Sky Karaköy carries a Seasonally Closed label on its own group's site, and Manifest advertises its glass ceiling precisely because staying open through the cold is unusual here. Between November and March, telephone the venue on the day. A confirmed booking is not proof the roof is trading. Roughly November to March · phone on the day, not the week before

quartiers|Kadıköy.name: Kadıköy
quartiers|Kadıköy.teaser: The shore an oracle called blind. It has the star now.
quartiers|Kadıköy.body: Megaran settlers founded Chalcedon on this headland seventeen years before Byzantium went up across the water — the oracle called them blind for choosing the wrong shore. Mehmed II gave the farmland to Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first Ottoman judge, and Chalcedon became kadı-köy , the judge's village. The joke has aged badly. Araf's star, Çiya's field-recording kitchen and the deepest Turkish wine list in the city are all on this side now, and the European side crosses over for dinner. Asian shore · vapur from Eminönü, Karaköy and Beşiktaş, about 20 minutes

quartiers|Moda.name: Moda
quartiers|Moda.teaser: Wooden villas built by three communities, and the pier that outlived them.
quartiers|Moda.body: The headland below Kadıköy, laid out in the late nineteenth century when Greek, Armenian and Levantine families built wooden summer houses down the lanes to the water. Their churches — Hagia Triada among them — still hold services; their congregations are a fraction of what they were. The Vedat Tek ferry pier of about 1917 has been restored as a book café and public library, and the coast path around the point is the best free hour on the Asian side. Walk it westward into the sunset. Moda, Kadıköy · 15 minutes on foot from Kadıköy pier, or the heritage tram loop

quartiers|Yeldeğirmeni.name: Yeldeğirmeni
quartiers|Yeldeğirmeni.teaser: Windmills, railway workers, and the first apartment blocks on this shore.
quartiers|Yeldeğirmeni.body: Named for the flour mills that once ground for the palace, and settled since the fifteenth century by Armenians, Greeks and Jews — a handful of families remain. It was the first quarter in Kadıköy to build apartment blocks instead of wooden houses, and several of the originals still stand on their streets. A mural programme covered the gable walls a decade ago; the coffee and the quieter rooms followed. Coffee Manifesto holds this end of the district. Go in the morning. Kadıköy, between the ferry pier and Haydarpaşa

quartiers|Üsküdar.name: Üsküdar
quartiers|Üsküdar.teaser: The gold city, and where the caravans set out for Mecca.
quartiers|Üsküdar.body: Megaran settlers again, this time calling it Chrysopolis, the golden city. Ottoman Üsküdar was the terminus of the Anatolian caravan routes and, for much of the Ottoman period, the point at which the Surre caravan left the mainland carrying the sultan's gifts to Mecca; the regular caravan ended in 1915. That made it Muslim, settled and sober while the rest of the city was mixed and licensed — which is why the lokantas here are superb and the meyhanes essentially absent. Asian shore · ferries from Eminönü and Beşiktaş

quartiers|Kuzguncuk.name: Kuzguncuk
quartiers|Kuzguncuk.teaser: A synagogue, an Armenian church and a mosque, all on one street.
quartiers|Kuzguncuk.body: Once a largely Jewish village on the Asian shore. Along İcadiye Caddesi stand a mosque, the Bet Yaakov synagogue of 1878, an Armenian church and Greek Orthodox ones. Almost none of those congregations still live here. It is the physical proof of everything this guide argues, and it takes ten minutes to walk. Asian shore, one stop north of Üsküdar · İcadiye Caddesi runs up from the water

quartiers|Beyoğlu / Pera.group: Pera and the hill above it
quartiers|Beyoğlu / Pera.name: Beyoğlu / Pera
quartiers|Beyoğlu / Pera.teaser: The avenue was called Grand Rue de Péra, and it was not Turkish.
quartiers|Beyoğlu / Pera.body: Pera is Greek for beyond — the quarter across the Golden Horn from the old city. Foreigners won the right to buy property here in 1867 and built the Grand Rue de Péra with it: arcades, apartment houses and hotels in every style the century could supply. The Cité de Péra of 1876 became the Çiçek Pasajı, its elegant shops turned into rough meyhanes with barrels for tables. İstiklal Caddesi runs Taksim to Tünel · Asmalımescit and Nevizade at its lower end

quartiers|Cihangir.group: Pera and the hill above it
quartiers|Cihangir.name: Cihangir
quartiers|Cihangir.teaser: A dead prince's mosque, then the writers, now the small serious rooms.
quartiers|Cihangir.body: Named for the mosque Sinan built in 1559 for Şehzade Cihangir, Süleyman's son, dead at twenty-two; the present building is an 1889 replacement after repeated fires and earthquakes. The slope below Taksim became the writers-and-cats quarter in the 1990s and has held that register better than most gentrified districts manage. Two rooms from this guide sit here: Casius, cooking Antakya food and carrying a 2026 Bib Gourmand, and Østre, the oyster and raw bar that opened this year. Beyoğlu, on the slope between Taksim and Fındıklı

quartiers|Nişantaşı.group: Pera and the hill above it
quartiers|Nişantaşı.name: Nişantaşı
quartiers|Nişantaşı.teaser: Named for the stones that recorded how far a sultan's arrow flew.
quartiers|Nişantaşı.body: A nişan taşı is an inscribed stele recording a record shot: Selim III's here dates from 1790–91, Mahmud II's from 1811. Mahmud II then encouraged settlement and the archery ground became the city's grandest residential grid. It is not a cooking quarter. It is a drinking and listening one — Lips for natural wine, and June and Dama in Teşvikiye next door, the second a café that turns hi-fi bar after dark. Şişli · runs into Teşvikiye and Harbiye

quartiers|Karaköy and Galata.name: Karaköy and Galata
quartiers|Karaköy and Galata.teaser: A Genoese city-state with its own walls, now the cruise front.
quartiers|Karaköy and Galata.body: Galata was a colony of the Republic of Genoa from 1267 to 1453 — walled, self-governing, and topped by the tower it finished in 1348. Five centuries later the banker Abraham Salomon Camondo cut his baroque staircase down to Bankalar Caddesi so he could walk from his house to his bank. Galataport reopened this waterfront to the public in 2021. Neolokal holds a star above it; the roof bars hold the view. Beyoğlu, at the mouth of the Golden Horn · Kamondo stairs off Bankalar Caddesi

quartiers|Balat.name: Balat
quartiers|Balat.teaser: Five centuries of Jewish Istanbul, sold now as a colour photograph.
quartiers|Balat.body: The name is probably from palation , palace, for the Blachernae ruins on the hill above. Sephardic and Romaniote families lived here for five centuries; the Ahrida synagogue, founded in the 1430s by Jews from Ohrid, is one of the oldest in the city and still in use. Agora Meyhanesi, which dates itself to 1890, is the reason to be here after dark. The painted staircases draw a queue by mid-morning, so do the lanes first and the photograph never. Fatih, on the Golden Horn · Ahrida synagogue visits by prior arrangement

quartiers|Fener.name: Fener
quartiers|Fener.teaser: The first throne of Orthodoxy, and a red school on the hill.
quartiers|Fener.body: Phanar, the lighthouse, named the quarter and then the Phanariots — the Greek families who supplied the Ottoman state its dragomans, its interpreters and its Danubian princes. The Ecumenical Patriarchate is still here, and above it stands the Phanar Greek Orthodox College, the Red Castle, built 1881–83 by the architect Konstantinos Dimadis at a recorded cost of 17,210 Ottoman gold pounds. The school itself opened in 1454, the year after the conquest. It has outlasted the community it was built to teach. Fatih, on the Golden Horn immediately north of Balat

quartiers|Arnavutköy.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages
quartiers|Arnavutköy.name: Arnavutköy
quartiers|Arnavutköy.teaser: The great current, an Albanian name, and a strawberry that lost its fields.
quartiers|Arnavutköy.body: Byzantine Mega Revma, the great current, for the water that runs fastest along this bank. Mehmed II resettled Albanians here in 1468 and the Turkish name followed, but the village stayed heavily Greek into the twentieth century, with Armenian and Jewish families beside them. It grew the Ottoman strawberry — small, less sweet than the modern berry, intensely scented — on forty hectares of hillside that are now streets. The bay-windowed wooden yalı are the best surviving row on the European shore. Tam Ocakbaşı cooks here. Beşiktaş, European shore · the waterside walk north to Bebek is about 3 km

quartiers|Bebek.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages
quartiers|Bebek.name: Bebek
quartiers|Bebek.teaser: A palace demoted to a consulate when the capital left.
quartiers|Bebek.body: The name means baby, and the bay is the calmest water on the European shore, which is why the yalı here belong to people who can afford calm. The white art nouveau pile on the front was built 1899–1901 for Emine Valide Pasha, mother of the last Khedive of Egypt; it became the Egyptian embassy and was later downgraded to a consulate once the capital moved to Ankara. The whole city's demotion, in one building. Beşiktaş, European shore · walk in from Arnavutköy along the water

quartiers|Tarabya.group: Up the strait — the Bosphorus villages
quartiers|Tarabya.name: Tarabya
quartiers|Tarabya.teaser: Poison, renamed cure, then rented to ambassadors.
quartiers|Tarabya.body: Byzantine Pharmakia — poison, after the Medea legend — until it was renamed Therapeia, the cure, for its springs; tradition credits Archbishop Atticus, some time between 406 and 425. It became the summer address of the embassies. Abdülhamid II gave the German one its plot in 1880; the residence went up between 1885 and 1887 and has run since 2011 as an artists' residency. The bay below is a fish-restaurant row, and Arogan, with Burak Zafer cooking, opened above it this year. Sarıyer, European shore · the far end of the Bosphorus road, north of Yeniköy

walks|Eminönü to Kadıköy.name: Eminönü to Kadıköy
walks|Eminönü to Kadıköy.teaser: The commute that happens to be the best twenty minutes in the city.
walks|Eminönü to Kadıköy.body: The line traces back to the Şirket-i Hayriye of 1851, the Ottoman empire's first joint-stock company; the boats today are run by Şehir Hatları, municipal since 2006 and working 32 lines from 53 piers. Take the open deck, order tea from the tray that never spills, and watch the old city separate from Galata as you pull out. It is transport rather than a tour, which is exactly why it is worth doing. Eminönü pier, Fatih · Şehir Hatları · pay with İstanbulkart, no ticket queue

walks|Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar.name: Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar
walks|Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar.teaser: The shortest hop to Asia — take it back westward with the sun going down.
walks|Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar.body: Üsküdar was Chrysopolis, founded by colonists from Megara in the seventh century BC, and for centuries the point at which Asia began: the caravan roads east and the pilgrim road to Mecca started from this shore. The Maiden's Tower stands offshore — a Byzantine tower of 1110 on a rock the Athenians had already used as a customs post, rebuilt repeatedly since; what you see is Ottoman. Sinan's Mihrimah Sultan mosque sits above the pier and his small Şemsi Paşa mosque almost in the water. Cross back westward at dusk and the European skyline lights up in front of you. Üsküdar pier · frequent all day · Şemsi Paşa mosque is a few minutes south along the water

walks|The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to.name: The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to Eyüpsultan
walks|The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to.tag: ~50 min end to end · hop off
walks|The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to.teaser: One boat, nine piers, and the door of every walk in the next group.
walks|The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to.body: The Haliç line runs Üsküdar, Karaköy, Kasımpaşa, Fener, Balat, Hasköy, Ayvansaray, Sütlüce, Eyüpsultan — which is to say it stops at the door of every walk in the next group. The Golden Horn is 7.5 km long and was an industrial sewer within living memory; the clean-up through the 1980s and 1990s is the reason you can now sit on deck and enjoy it. Ride to the top, walk, and come back by boat. Board at Üsküdar or Karaköy · alight at Fener or Balat · same İstanbulkart fare

walks|Arnavutköy to Bebek.name: Arnavutköy to Bebek
walks|Arnavutköy to Bebek.teaser: Painted timber houses on the water, then a bay full of boats.
walks|Arnavutköy to Bebek.body: Arnavutköy means Albanian village — by tradition Mehmed II settled Albanians here after 1453. The painted timber houses standing straight out of the water, late nineteenth and early twentieth century with Art Nouveau fronts, line the shore road. Walk north along it into Bebek, past the Egyptian consulate, raised 1899 to 1901 for the mother of Egypt's last khedive, and stop at the bay. START Arnavutköy pier, north along the shore road · free · flat throughout, no shade at midday

walks|Kuzguncuk's one street.name: Kuzguncuk's one street
walks|Kuzguncuk's one street.teaser: A mosque, a synagogue and a church on the same short road.
walks|Kuzguncuk's one street.body: İcadiye Caddesi runs a few hundred metres up from the water, and along it stand a mosque, the Bet Yaakov synagogue — conventionally dated 1878 and probably older — an Armenian church and Greek Orthodox ones. Sephardic Jews settled here after the expulsions from Spain; the oldest Jewish gravestone in the neighbourhood is dated 1562. The community thinned after 1948 and emptied fast after the 1955 pogrom, replaced by migrants from the Black Sea coast. One street, the whole argument. START Kuzguncuk pier, or a short bus north from Üsküdar · free · residential — keep the volume down

walks|Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk.name: Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk
walks|Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk.teaser: The flat seafront the Asian side actually uses, pointed at the sunset.
walks|Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk.body: Moda became fashionable from the 1870s as a summer quarter for Greek, Armenian and Levantine families, which is why Greek Orthodox, Anglican and Catholic churches and the 1870 Lycée Saint-Joseph still stand among the apartment blocks. The pier building dates from 1917 and was restored in 2022. Walk out to Moda Burnu, sit on the grass with everyone else and watch the sun drop behind the Historic Peninsula. The nostalgia tram loops back into Kadıköy. START Kadıköy pier, south along the shore · free · Kadıköy–Moda nostalgia tram runs the loop back

walks|Fener — the Patriarchate and the R.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
walks|Fener — the Patriarchate and the R.name: Fener — the Patriarchate and the Red Castle
walks|Fener — the Patriarchate and the R.teaser: Orthodoxy's senior see, on a back street, behind an iron gate.
walks|Fener — the Patriarchate and the R.body: The Ecumenical Patriarchate has sat here since about 1600, and the Phanariot Greeks of this quarter supplied the Ottoman state its dragomans and, between 1711 and 1821, the governors of Wallachia and Moldavia. Above it rises the vast red-brick Phanar Greek Orthodox College, which now has almost no pupils, and that is the plainest measure of what happened here. Nearby, St Mary of the Mongols is the only Byzantine church in the city that has never stopped being a Greek Orthodox place of worship; the firmans of Mehmed II and Bayezid II granting it to the Greek community still hang there. Fener pier on the Haliç line · St George's Cathedral free, modest dress · the college is not open to visitors

walks|The iron church of St Stephen.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
walks|The iron church of St Stephen.name: The iron church of St Stephen
walks|The iron church of St Stephen.teaser: A church cast in Vienna, shipped down the Danube, bolted together here.
walks|The iron church of St Stephen.body: The Bulgarians broke from the Greek Patriarchate in 1870 and wanted a church of their own. The Ottoman Armenian architect Hovsep Aznavur drew it on an iron frame because the ground here is soft; the Austrian firm R. Ph. Waagner cast some 500 tonnes of parts in Vienna between 1893 and 1896 and shipped them down the Danube and across the Black Sea. Consecrated 8 September 1898, restored 2011 to 2018. A whole church made of metal. Mürselpaşa Caddesi, on the shore road between Fener and Balat piers · free

walks|Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quar.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
walks|Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quar.name: Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quarter
walks|Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quar.teaser: Eighteen synagogues once; three still working, one with a bimah shaped like a prow.
walks|Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quar.body: Bayezid II opened the city to Jews fleeing the Spanish Inquisition after 1492 and Balat became the centre of Istanbul's Jewish life, with eighteen synagogues at its height. Ahrida was founded in the fifteenth century by Jews from Ohrid; its wooden bimah is built in the shape of a boat's prow, and Sabbatai Zevi prayed here — the only Istanbul synagogue where he did. He had proclaimed himself the Messiah at Smyrna at Rosh Hashanah in 1665, and on reaching Constantinople in February 1666 he was arrested on the order of the grand vizier Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha. Three synagogues still work. Balat is now overwhelmingly Muslim, and in the 2020s heavily gentrified. Kürkçü Çeşme Sokak, Balat · synagogue visits only by prior arrangement through the Jewish community · steep streets

walks|Eyüpsultan and the hill above it.group: The Golden Horn, pier by pier
walks|Eyüpsultan and the hill above it.name: Eyüpsultan and the hill above it
walks|Eyüpsultan and the hill above it.teaser: A pilgrimage mosque, a cemetery up the slope, and a cable car to the view.
walks|Eyüpsultan and the hill above it.body: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, a companion of the Prophet, died during the Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s. His tomb was declared rediscovered after 1453, and the mosque raised over it became the place where each new sultan was girded with the Sword of Osman. It is a working pilgrimage site, so dress for it and avoid Friday midday. Above, the cemetery climbs to the Pierre Loti café, named for the French novelist and reached by cable car. Eyüpsultan pier at the head of the Golden Horn · mosque free, modest dress · teleferik up to the café

walks|Büyükada by ferry.name: Büyükada by ferry
walks|Büyükada by ferry.teaser: Five and a half square kilometres with no engine noise in them.
walks|Büyükada by ferry.body: The Byzantines exiled inconvenient royals here, which is where the name comes from. A 1912 census counted roughly 10,250 Greeks to 670 Turks across the nine islands; this was a Greek, Armenian and Jewish summer world and it is not one now. Private cars are still banned. The horse phaetons have gone too: an outbreak of glanders among the horses finished them, and an Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality council decision of 16 January 2020 ended the phaeton era for good, with electric vehicles taking over the same summer. Ferries from Kabataş, Beşiktaş and Eminönü (about 90 min) or Bostancı and Kadıköy (about 45) · bicycles for hire at the pier

walks|The Monastery of St George.name: The Monastery of St George
walks|The Monastery of St George.teaser: A steep climb that Muslims and Christians make together on the saint's day.
walks|The Monastery of St George.body: Aya Yorgi sits at the island's highest point, 203 metres up. A chapel of 1751 stood here; the present cut-stone church was begun in 1905 and finished in 1909. The origin story — icons buried during a medieval sack and rediscovered after a shepherd's dream — is the standard one for a Greek shrine. What is not standard is the crowd: on 23 April, St George's day, thousands climb the path, and a great many of them are Muslim. Yücetepe, Büyükada · walk up from Birlik Meydanı, roughly 40 min · steep, no shade, carry water

walks|The Prinkipo Orphanage.name: The Prinkipo Orphanage
walks|The Prinkipo Orphanage.teaser: Europe's largest wooden building, twenty thousand square metres of it, empty since 1964.
walks|The Prinkipo Orphanage.body: Alexandre Vallaury designed it in 1898 for the Wagons-Lits company as the Prinkipo Palace, a hotel and casino for Orient Express passengers. Abdülhamid II refused the licence; a Greek banker's wife bought it and gave it to the Patriarchate, and it opened as an orphanage on 21 May 1903. Turkish authorities forced it shut on 21 April 1964, the year of the expulsions. Confiscated in 1997, returned after Strasbourg ruled against Turkey. In the pines above Büyükada, on the way up to Aya Yorgi · closed and unsafe — look from outside only

walks|Heybeliada and the closed seminary.name: Heybeliada and the closed seminary
walks|Heybeliada and the closed seminary.teaser: The school that trained a thousand priests, closed by a law about colleges.
walks|Heybeliada and the closed seminary.body: The Theological School of Halki opened on 1 October 1844 on the hill above Heybeliada and turned out close to a thousand priests, bishops and patriarchs. In 1971 Turkish legislation banning private higher education closed it, and it has taken no student since — though Ankara and the Patriarchate announced in 2026 that it will reopen. American presidents and the EU have pressed for that for decades. The monastery keeps the building, the library and the view. Get off one island early. Hill above Heybeliada pier · the grounds are not a public museum — access is occasional and by arrangement · quieter than Büyükada

walks|The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı.group: Out of the city for a day
walks|The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı.name: The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı
walks|The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı.teaser: The whole strait end to end, on a commuter boat with a lunch stop.
walks|The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı.body: The long Şehir Hatları service runs from Eminönü to Anadolu Kavağı at the northern mouth of the Bosphorus, calling at Sarıyer and Rumeli Kavağı, and holds at the top long enough for lunch before turning back. Above the village stands Yoros Castle, fortified under the late Byzantines, Ottoman from 1391, lost to Genoa in 1414 for forty years — which is why everyone calls it the Genoese castle — then refortified by Mehmed II. Departs Eminönü Boğaz İskelesi · twice daily · the village is a row of fish restaurants and prices there are tourist-grade

walks|Belgrad Forest.group: Out of the city for a day
walks|Belgrad Forest.name: Belgrad Forest
walks|Belgrad Forest.teaser: The oak forest north of the city, and the waterworks that supplied Ottoman Istanbul.
walks|Belgrad Forest.body: The name is literal: Süleyman deported thousands of Serbs from Belgrade to the capital in 1521, and the village they were settled in named the forest. Two Ottoman systems ran through it — the sixteenth-century Kırkçeşme network upgraded by Sinan, and the eighteenth-century Taksim one — and their dams and aqueducts, among them the Maglova aqueduct and the Mahmud I arch of 1732, still stand among the sessile oaks. Some 5,500 hectares, with a 6.5 km running loop. Bahçeköy, Sarıyer · about an hour from the centre by road · Büyük Bent is the busiest gate · go early, it fills at weekends

culture|Hagia Sophia.name: Hagia Sophia
culture|Hagia Sophia.teaser: The dome came down once already, and the one overhead is the replacement.
culture|Hagia Sophia.body: Justinian's church was inaugurated on 27 December 537, built in five years and ten months by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. The first dome fell in the earthquake of 7 May 558; Isidore the Younger rebuilt it higher and steeper by 562, and that is the dome overhead. Cathedral for nine centuries, mosque from 1453, museum from 1935, mosque again since July 2020. Sultanahmet · the EUR 25 ticket covers the upper gallery; the ground floor is a working prayer hall and closes to visitors around the five daily prayers

culture|Chora — Kariye Mosque.name: Chora — Kariye Mosque
culture|Chora — Kariye Mosque.teaser: The finest Byzantine mosaic cycle anywhere, and three panels of it are behind curtains.
culture|Chora — Kariye Mosque.body: Theodore Metochites, Grand Logothete under Andronikos II, paid for the mosaics and frescoes between about 1315 and 1321 and had himself worked into the panel above the door, handing the church over to Christ. He later fell from power and died as a monk inside it. Converted to a mosque in the early sixteenth century, made a museum in 1945, returned to worship and reopened on 6 May 2024 after four years of restoration. The narthex cycles are all visible; the figural mosaics in the prayer hall are veiled. Edirnekapı, Fatih · daily 09:00-18:00; no visitor entry on Fridays or during the five daily prayers

culture|Süleymaniye Mosque.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
culture|Süleymaniye Mosque.teaser: Sinan piped the lamp smoke into one room and turned the soot into ink.
culture|Süleymaniye Mosque.body: Begun 1550, finished 1557, and never only a mosque: it came with four madrasas, a medical school, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a caravanserai and a hamam. Süleyman lies in the garden tomb, Hürrem Sultan in hers of 1558, and Sinan in a small tomb at the corner of the wall he built. Above the entrance he set a chamber that drew oil-lamp smoke off the walls; the collected soot went to the palace calligraphers. Süleymaniye, Fatih · free entry, closed to visitors around the five prayers · one of the four zones UNESCO inscribed as the Historic Areas of Istanbul in 1985

culture|Topkapı Palace.name: Topkapı Palace
culture|Topkapı Palace.teaser: The Quran is read aloud, all day, in the room that has held the relics since 1517.
culture|Topkapı Palace.body: Mehmed II ordered construction from 1459; the palace was finished around 1478 and governed the empire until the court moved to Dolmabahçe in 1856. The Chamber of the Sacred Relics has held its collection since 1517, when Selim I took Cairo and the caliphate came north — and the practice of recitation came with it, kept now by a rota of readers through opening hours. In the Treasury: the Topkapı dagger and the eighty-six-carat Spoonmaker's Diamond. Sultanahmet · 09:00-17:30, closed Tuesdays · one combined ticket now covers the palace, the Harem and Hagia Irene

culture|Basilica Cistern.name: Basilica Cistern
culture|Basilica Cistern.teaser: Two Medusa heads used as furniture, one on her side, one upside down.
culture|Basilica Cistern.body: Justinian's reservoir was built around 532 beneath a public basilica, which is where the name comes from. Three hundred and thirty-six columns, most of them scavenged from older buildings, carried water to the Great Palace above. In the north-west corner two carved Medusa heads serve as column bases, one laid sideways, one inverted, with no surviving explanation for either. It reopened in July 2022 after five years of restoration and seismic strengthening; management passed to the state foundations body in June 2026, which briefly closed it. Yerebatan Cad., Sultanahmet · daily 09:00-18:30, night visit 19:30-22:00 · cards and İstanbulkart only, no cash

culture|Istanbul Archaeological Museums.name: Istanbul Archaeological Museums
culture|Istanbul Archaeological Museums.teaser: The painter who dug up the Alexander Sarcophagus then built a museum around it.
culture|Istanbul Archaeological Museums.body: Osman Hamdi Bey excavated the royal necropolis at Sidon in 1887 and brought back a Pentelic marble sarcophagus with its painted surfaces still partly legible — Macedonian and Persian figures fighting in colour. The museum he founded around the find opened on 13 June 1891 and holds roughly a million objects, among them two of the three tablets of the Kadesh treaty of about 1259 BC, the oldest known peace treaty; the United Nations hangs a copy in New York. Osman Hamdi Bey Yokuşu, Gülhane, Fatih · entered from the first court of Topkapı or from Gülhane Park; ticketed separately from the palace

culture|Istanbul Modern.name: Istanbul Modern
culture|Istanbul Modern.teaser: A viewing terrace hovering over a sheet of water covering the whole roof.
culture|Istanbul Modern.body: Founded in 2004 as Türkiye's first museum of modern and contemporary art, it started in a Karaköy warehouse, moved out in 2018, and returned to the same stretch of waterfront on 4 May 2023 in Renzo Piano's first building in the country. The aluminium facade is cut to catch the strait's light. On the roof a terrace stands above a shallow reflecting plane, so the water on the building and the water below run together. Semiha Berksoy's retrospective closes 6 September 2026. Tophane İskele Cad. 1/1, Beyoğlu (Galataport) · Tue-Thu and Sat-Sun 10:00-18:00, Fri to 20:00, closed Mondays

culture|Pera Museum.name: Pera Museum
culture|Pera Museum.teaser: An 1893 hotel that now owns the record-breaking Turkish painting.
culture|Pera Museum.body: The building opened in 1893 as the Bristol, one of the Pera hotels that took Orient Express traffic alongside the Pera Palace and the Tokatlıyan. Its facade was kept and everything behind it rebuilt as galleries; the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation opened the museum on 8 June 2005. The anchor is Osman Hamdi Bey's The Tortoise Trainer , painted in 1906 and bought at auction in December 2004 for a sum that was then a record for a Turkish work. Meşrutiyet Cad., Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu · Tue-Sat 10:00-19:00 (Fri to 22:00), Sun 12:00-18:00, closed Mondays · free Fridays 18:00-22:00, free for students on Wednesdays

culture|SALT Galata.name: SALT Galata
culture|SALT Galata.teaser: The Imperial Ottoman Bank's head office, and it costs nothing to walk in.
culture|SALT Galata.body: Alexandre Vallaury finished the Imperial Ottoman Bank's headquarters on Bankalar Caddesi in 1892, and the bank held the building until 1999. SALT took it in November 2011 and made it free: galleries, an open research library, a café and bookshop at street level, and the Ottoman Bank archive covering 145 years downstairs. Bankalar Cad. 11, Karaköy · Tue-Sat 11:00-19:00, Sun 11:00-18:00, closed Mondays · free admission

culture|Çiçek Pasajı.name: Çiçek Pasajı
culture|Çiçek Pasajı.teaser: Built on the ashes of the empire's opera house, named after Russian refugees.
culture|Çiçek Pasajı.body: The Naum Theatre stood here — the Ottoman capital's chief opera house, staging Verdi, with Sultans Abdülaziz and Abdülhamid II in the audience — until the Pera fire of 1870. The Greek banker Hristaki Zoğrafos bought the ruin and had Kleanthis Zannos build the Cité de Péra on it in 1876: twenty-four shops below, eighteen apartments above. Destitute Russian noblewomen who arrived after 1917 sold flowers in the corridor, and by the 1940s the name had stuck. The building failed in 1978 and was rebuilt by 1988. The clientele was not. İstiklal Caddesi at Galatasaray, Beyoğlu · further restoration work in 2005 and 2022

culture|Zeki Müren.name: Zeki Müren
culture|Zeki Müren.teaser: Turkey's most beloved voice belonged to its most flamboyant man, and nobody minded.
culture|Zeki Müren.body: Born in Bursa, schooled in Istanbul, he entered the State Academy of Fine Arts in 1950 and made his first live broadcast on Istanbul Radio on 1 January 1951. He then held the stage at the Maksim gazino in Taksim for eleven years — the big-room, orchestra-backed successor to the meyhane's fasıl nights. A sequinned jacket from 1958, a miniskirt from 1970, and no loss of affection from a conservative public. He collapsed and died at a TRT ceremony on 24 September 1996, leaving everything to two charitable foundations. Taksim · the Maksim gazino closed in 2005 and the site is now a hotel

culture|Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanag.name: Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanage
culture|Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanag.teaser: Europe's largest wooden building, shut by the state in 1964 and empty since.
culture|Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanag.body: Alexandre Vallaury — the architect of the Ottoman Bank — built it in 1898 for the Wagons-Lits company, which ran the Orient Express, as a hotel and casino. Abdülhamid II refused the operating permit. In 1903 Eleni Zarifi bought it and gave it to the Ecumenical Patriarchate, which ran it as an orphanage for Greek children until Turkish authorities forced it shut on 21 April 1964. Twenty thousand square metres of timber have stood open to the weather since. Title was returned in 2012; a restoration partnership was signed in June 2026. Büyükada, Princes' Islands · uphill from the pier; the building is closed and derelict, so this is an exterior

culture|Yenikapı — the dig that held up.name: Yenikapı — the dig that held up the railway
culture|Yenikapı — the dig that held up.teaser: Digging the Bosphorus rail tunnel turned up a settlement 8,500 years old.
culture|Yenikapı — the dig that held up.body: Salvage excavation at Yenikapı ran from 2004 to 2013 and held the Marmaray project up for years. It exposed the Theodosian Harbour and thirty-seven shipwrecks of the fifth to eleventh centuries, the largest group of medieval ships ever found on a single site. Below the harbour floor came something much older: dwelling foundations, burials and human footprints from roughly 8,500 years ago, when the Sea of Marmara was still a lake. Sixty thousand objects in all. Yenikapı, Fatih — now a transport interchange · the finds are held by the Istanbul Archaeological Museums

culture|Halfdan's runes.name: Halfdan's runes
culture|Halfdan's runes.teaser: A Varangian guardsman got bored during a service and carved his name.
culture|Halfdan's runes.body: In 1964 a runic inscription about twenty-three centimetres long was found scratched into the marble parapet of Hagia Sophia's upper south gallery. Only the ending, -ftan, is legible; runologists read it as Halfdan and reconstruct the ordinary Norse formula behind it — Halfdan carved these runes. He would have been one of the Varangians, the Norse and later Anglo-Saxon mercenaries who guarded Byzantine emperors from the late tenth century. A second name, Ári, surfaced in 1975. Upper south gallery — inside the ticketed visiting route, not the prayer floor

culture|Tünel.name: Tünel
culture|Tünel.teaser: Twelve years after London, the second underground railway on earth — 573 metres.
culture|Tünel.body: The French engineer Eugène-Henri Gavand built it to solve exactly one problem: the climb from the port at Galata to the merchant quarter at Pera. It opened on 17 January 1875, which makes it the second-oldest underground urban railway in the world after the London Underground of 1863. Five hundred and seventy-three metres of it, about sixty of them vertical. It ran on steam until the renovation that closed the line in 1968; electrified and reopened in 1971, it is still doing the only job it was built for. Karaköy to Tünel Meydanı, Beyoğlu · two stations, a ride of well under two minutes · İstanbulkart accepted

culture|The Obelisk of Theodosius.name: The Obelisk of Theodosius
culture|The Obelisk of Theodosius.teaser: Already eighteen centuries old when Constantinople put it up.
culture|The Obelisk of Theodosius.body: The granite was cut for Thutmose III and raised at Karnak, its inscriptions marking his campaign to the Euphrates around 1450 BC. Theodosius I had it shipped from Egypt and re-erected on the spine of the Hippodrome in 390 AD. It lost length in transit, so what stands is the upper section, 18.5 metres of it, on a marble base carved in Constantinople showing the emperor watching the races from his box. Nothing else in the city comes close in age. Sultanahmet Meydanı (At Meydanı) · outdoors, free, at any hour

culture|The Black Russian.name: The Black Russian
culture|The Black Russian.teaser: The man who brought jazz to Istanbul was born in Mississippi to freed slaves.
culture|The Black Russian.body: Frederick Bruce Thomas was born in Coahoma County, Mississippi in November 1872 to parents who had been enslaved. He reached Moscow by way of London, ran theatres and restaurants there for nineteen years, and fled the revolution to Constantinople. By Vladimir Alexandrov's account he opened Stella in Şişli, then Maxim in Taksim in 1921, and the city heard the foxtrot, the Charleston and live jazz through him. Refused a United States passport and buried in debt, he died in a debtors' prison in June 1928. Şişli and Taksim · the Maksim name outlived him on Taksim until 2005 · biography: Vladimir Alexandrov, The Black Russian

coffee-gardens|Türk kahvesi.name: Türk kahvesi
coffee-gardens|Türk kahvesi.teaser: Two Syrians opened the first coffeehouse here in 1554; the city never recovered.
coffee-gardens|Türk kahvesi.body: Hakem of Aleppo and Şems of Damascus opened Istanbul's first kahvehane in Tahtakale in 1554. Around fifty were counted in the city by the end of Süleyman's reign; Murad IV later banned the drink outright, on the correct assumption that men who sit together talk. UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture in 2013 for the ritual rather than the bean: water first, a sweet alongside, the grounds left in the cup for the fal. ORDER sade, az şekerli, orta or çok şekerli — the sugar goes in before the boil, never after

coffee-gardens|Çay, and the tulip glass.name: Çay, and the tulip glass
coffee-gardens|Çay, and the tulip glass.teaser: A law of 1924 put tea on the Black Sea coast, and it took over the whole day.
coffee-gardens|Çay, and the tulip glass.body: Law 407 of 1924 put tea cultivation on a legal footing at Rize on the wet Black Sea coast; the aim Çaykur records is work and income for the Eastern Black Sea after the First World War. The first large harvest came in 1938, the first factory in 1947. It is served in the ince belli, the thin-waisted glass, held by the rim — and refusing one is close to rude. Ask for açık (weak) or koyu (strong); the stacked double pot lets the server mix it to order

coffee-gardens|Kahvaltı — the word.name: Kahvaltı — the word
coffee-gardens|Kahvaltı — the word.teaser: Breakfast here is literally named 'under coffee', and the coffee has since vanished.
coffee-gardens|Kahvaltı — the word.body: Kahve altı, 'under coffee', was the small thing eaten before the cup, on the reasoning that Turkish coffee on an empty stomach is punishing. The two words fused into one and the term is first recorded in the 1870s. The meal then outgrew its own name — twenty small plates, three hours, no hurry — and the drink beside it is now tea. The word is a fossil of a coffee city that switched. The full spread is serpme kahvaltı; Sunday, late morning, and plan nothing afterwards

coffee-gardens|Çınaraltı, Çengelköy.name: Çınaraltı, Çengelköy
coffee-gardens|Çınaraltı, Çengelköy.teaser: Chairs set under a plane tree said to be nearly a thousand years old.
coffee-gardens|Çınaraltı, Çengelköy.body: The name means 'under the plane tree', and the tree is the entire proposition: a vast çınar on the Asian shore at Çengelköy, its canopy over tables facing the water. The garden pours tea and coffee and nothing else — you are expected to bring your own food, and people do, in bags. No music, no backgammon, no nargile, open at any hour. It is the least commercial room in this guide. Çengelköy waterfront, Üsküdar — Asian shore · tea and coffee only, bring your own food

coffee-gardens|Pierre Loti Kahvesi.name: Pierre Loti Kahvesi
coffee-gardens|Pierre Loti Kahvesi.teaser: A hilltop coffeehouse from the 1800s, above the graves, looking down the Golden Horn.
coffee-gardens|Pierre Loti Kahvesi.body: Evliya Çelebi knew this hill as the İdris Köşkü picnic ground. By the nineteenth century a coffeehouse called Rabia Kadın stood on it, and the French naval officer Julien Viaud — writing as Pierre Loti — arrived in 1876 and is said to have finished Aziyadé at one of its tables. The hill took his name. Ride the cable car up from Eyüp pier, then walk back down through the Ottoman cemetery: that descent is the reason to come. İdris Köşkü Cad., Eyüpsultan · teleferik from Eyüp pier, about three minutes · busiest at sunset

coffee-gardens|Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi.name: Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi
coffee-gardens|Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi.teaser: The whole of Kadıköy, three generations of it, facing the Marmara over a backgammon board.
coffee-gardens|Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi.body: A municipal tea garden on the slope above Moda's shore: umbrellas and plastic chairs under tall trees, the Sea of Marmara filling the view with the Princes' Islands on the horizon. Nobody is performing. Grandparents, students and dog-walkers hold tables for hours over tea and tavla, the food runs to sandwiches and toast, and half the room brought its own. This is what the Asian side does with an afternoon. Caferağa, Park İçi Yolu, Moda, Kadıköy · outdoor only, so weather decides · late afternoon into sunset

coffee-gardens|Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medreses.name: Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medresesi
coffee-gardens|Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medreses.teaser: A theology college courtyard where the students were replaced by nargile smoke.
coffee-gardens|Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medreses.body: Çorlulu Ali Paşa built this medrese in 1708 on the old Divanyolu, the imperial processional road, as a working college. Its two courtyards now hold carpet dealers and one of the city's long-standing nargile and tea gardens — low stools, cushions, glasses arriving without being asked. It is the single good reason to sit down in the old city, which this guide otherwise tells you to eat your way out of. Yeniçeriler Cd. (old Divanyolu), Beyazıt, Fatih — between the Grand Bazaar and Çemberlitaş · tea and nargile, no alcohol

coffee-gardens|İnci Pastanesi.name: İnci Pastanesi
coffee-gardens|İnci Pastanesi.teaser: One dessert, one recipe, since the 1940s — then redevelopment moved the whole shop.
coffee-gardens|İnci Pastanesi.body: İnci opened in the Cercle d'Orient building on İstiklal in the mid-1940s and built the business on one thing: choux balls filled with pastry cream under a chocolate sauce, the profiterol. It is the version every other one in the country is measured against. The shop was evicted in the early 2010s when the building was redeveloped; it went dark for about seventy days and reopened round the corner on Mis Sokak. Mis Sok. 18/A, Beyoğlu · roughly 08:00 to midnight, daily · order the profiterol and nothing else

coffee-gardens|Markiz (ex-Lebon).name: Markiz (ex-Lebon)
coffee-gardens|Markiz (ex-Lebon).teaser: Four Art Nouveau seasons were ordered from France; two are still on the wall.
coffee-gardens|Markiz (ex-Lebon).body: Lebon's patisserie was trading on the Grand Rue from the 1880s and became the salon of Pera, with Pierre Loti and Yahya Kemal among the regulars. Its Art Nouveau faience panels were ordered from France: four seasons commissioned, and only Spring and Autumn survive in the room. When Lebon moved across the street in 1940, Avedis Ohanyan Çakır opened Markiz in the room it left, keeping the tiles. It closed in 1980 and came back, panels and all, in 2003. İstiklal Cad. 360–362, Beyoğlu, at the corner of the Oriental passage · grand-café prices, not budget coffee

coffee-gardens|Montag Coffee Roasters.name: Montag Coffee Roasters
coffee-gardens|Montag Coffee Roasters.teaser: Own-roasted beans across three rooms, and the Kadıköy one is where you sit down.
coffee-gardens|Montag Coffee Roasters.body: Montag roasts its own and runs rooms in Kadıköy, Moda and Bomonti. The Kadıköy shop is the one to sit in: counter downstairs, a quiet second floor, V60 and cold brew alongside espresso, and the kind of turnover that means the bag you buy was roasted recently. Beans by the bag if you are travelling on. Caferağa, Muvakkıthane Cd. 16/A, Kadıköy · 10:00–22:00, to 23:00 Fri–Sat · Baylan is at number 9 on the same street

coffee-gardens|Federal Galata.name: Federal Galata
coffee-gardens|Federal Galata.teaser: An Australian flat white at the top of a staircase built by Ottoman bankers.
coffee-gardens|Federal Galata.body: Sam Ceviköz and Levent Koçarslan were born in Istanbul and learned the trade in Australia, which is precisely what the room tastes like: filter, cold brew and a properly pulled flat white, no ceremony. It stands a few steps above the Camondo Stairs, the neo-baroque flight paid for in the 1870s by Abraham Salomon Camondo, the Sephardic banker of Galata, so his grandchildren could reach school in Pera. The bank is gone. The stairs are not. Şahkulu, Küçük Hendek Cd. 7, Galata, Beyoğlu · mornings · terrace seating on the slope

coffee-gardens|Dama.name: Dama
coffee-gardens|Dama.tag: Café by day · hi-fi by night
coffee-gardens|Dama.teaser: Filter coffee and laptops until the record shelf takes the room back.
coffee-gardens|Dama.body: On a Teşvikiye side street: open kitchen, ceramic surfaces, shelves of records, breakfast from nine, and enough tolerance for a laptop that the neighbourhood works here. Come evening the same room becomes a hi-fi bar — vinyl through proper equipment, DJs, cocktails built on things like macadamia and banana. Istanbul has taken to the listening-bar format faster than any other European city, and Dama is where you can watch the switch happen in one afternoon. Teşvikiye, Şakayık Sok. 19, Şişli · breakfast 09:00–13:00 weekdays, to 14:00 at weekends · no reservations

coffee-gardens|Neroli Daylight Kitchen.name: Neroli Daylight Kitchen
coffee-gardens|Neroli Daylight Kitchen.teaser: A kitchen that shuts at six on purpose and makes everything on the plate itself.
coffee-gardens|Neroli Daylight Kitchen.body: Neroli is the essential oil pressed from bitter-orange blossom, and the room runs at the same register: daylight, a short seasonal card, handmade croissants, soft breads to its own recipe, gelato. The charcuterie and the cured salmon are made in the kitchen rather than bought in, which is the actual difference here. It shuts at six and does not pretend to become a bar. In a district gone heavily to brunch theatre, that is the correction. Teşvikiye, Av. Süreyya Ağaoğlu Sok. 31/A, Şişli · Tue–Sun 09:00–18:00, closed Mondays

coffee-gardens|Mornings in Pera.name: Mornings in Pera
coffee-gardens|Mornings in Pera.teaser: The long Turkish breakfast, run as a proper kitchen rather than a photo set.
coffee-gardens|Mornings in Pera.body: The room sits in Asmalımescit, the old meyhane grid, and serves the sprawled kahvaltı across the middle of the day rather than for one crowded hour — its own bakery, breakfast running to four in the afternoon. The queue is the price of that: come at nine, or come at three and take the last long table of the day. Asmalı Mescit, Beyoğlu · breakfast 09:00–16:00 daily

coffee-gardens|Atatürk Kitaplığı.name: Atatürk Kitaplığı
coffee-gardens|Atatürk Kitaplığı.teaser: A free reading room in Beyoğlu, open until nine, seven days a week.
coffee-gardens|Atatürk Kitaplığı.body: Sedad Hakkı Eldem — the architect who spent a career folding the Ottoman timber house into modernism — drew this as a culture complex of library, museum and exhibition halls; only the library was ever built. Koç Holding put the building up in 1973 and the collection moved in on 3 March 1981: around 228,000 books, 20,000 periodicals and 10,000 bound volumes of newspapers, alongside manuscripts, maps, albums and postcards. The city runs it, entry is free, and the hours do not move for the weekend — 09:00 to 21:00, every day. Gümüşsuyu, Miralay Şefikbey Sok. No:6, Beyoğlu · every day 09:00–21:00 · free

coffee-gardens|SALT Research, SALT Galat.name: SALT Research, SALT Galata
coffee-gardens|SALT Research, SALT Galat.teaser: A bank built for the Galata money, emptied of it, handed to readers.
coffee-gardens|SALT Research, SALT Galat.body: Alexandre Vallaury built this as the headquarters of the Imperial Ottoman Bank, finished in 1892, and the bank worked from it until 1999. Han Tümertekin's conversion reopened the building in November 2011 as SALT Galata, holding the research library and the old Ottoman Bank Museum. Reading costs nothing, but SALT Research is a registered collection rather than a walk-in one: you sign up once and are issued a personal access pass, study areas are bookable in blocks of up to three hours, and nothing circulates. Outside, the stairs cut around 1870–1880 by Abraham Salomon Camondo, of the Ottoman-Venetian Jewish banking family whose street this was, still climb the hill. Maksut Aşkar's one-star Neolokal is upstairs in the same building. Bankalar Caddesi 11, Karaköy 34421 · SALT Research Tue–Sat 11:00–19:00 · free, registration required · closed Mondays

coffee-gardens|Kronotrop, Cihangir.group: Counters with the hours for it
coffee-gardens|Kronotrop, Cihangir.name: Kronotrop, Cihangir
coffee-gardens|Kronotrop, Cihangir.teaser: Sixteen hours a day of table, on the slope above Tophane.
coffee-gardens|Kronotrop, Cihangir.body: Kronotrop opened in 2012 as one of the first specialty roasteries in Turkey — its founder, Çağatay Gülabioğlu, was the country's first Q grader — and the Cihangir room is the flagship, on the slope above Tophane where a good share of the city's writers, editors and film people live. It runs 07:00 to 23:30, seven days a week. It is small and it fills, so the etiquette is one long session rather than a whole day at the same table. The chain has since passed forty branches across Turkey and beyond, with very different hours at each, so aim for this room rather than the nearest sign. Cihangir, Beyoğlu · daily 07:00–23:30

coffee-gardens|Petra Roasting Co., Bebek.group: Counters with the hours for it
coffee-gardens|Petra Roasting Co., Bebek.name: Petra Roasting Co., Bebek
coffee-gardens|Petra Roasting Co., Bebek.teaser: Where the shore walk ends and the morning's work starts.
coffee-gardens|Petra Roasting Co., Bebek.body: The walk north from Arnavutköy along the water, past the wooden yalı , ends in Bebek — and this branch opens at half past seven on weekdays, which makes it the obvious place to put a morning after the best hour on the European shore. It is closed on Mondays, so build the walk around a Tuesday. Four further branches sit at Gayrettepe, Şişhane, Topağacı and Maslak if you are on the wrong side of the hill; the Şişhane one also closes Mondays, the rest do not. Bebek, Beşiktaş · Tue–Fri 07:30–20:00 · Sat–Sun 10:00–20:00 · closed Mondays

coffee-gardens|Kubbeli Saloon, Pera Pala.name: Kubbeli Saloon, Pera Palace
coffee-gardens|Kubbeli Saloon, Pera Pala.teaser: Built for people who had just spent three days on a train.
coffee-gardens|Kubbeli Saloon, Pera Pala.body: Vallaury again: he began the hotel in 1892 and it opened in 1895, built to lodge Orient Express passengers arriving off the Paris run. It carried the first electric lift in Constantinople — reportedly the second in Europe — and Atatürk's Room 101 is kept as a museum room. The domed saloon pours a traditional afternoon tea every day from three until six, with live piano. It is priced the way a grand hotel prices things: an hour of reading and correspondence, not a working day. Meşrutiyet Caddesi, Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu · afternoon tea daily 15:00–18:00

coffee-gardens|Istanbul Modern.name: Istanbul Modern
coffee-gardens|Istanbul Modern.teaser: Renzo Piano put a pool on the roof and the city behind it.
coffee-gardens|Istanbul Modern.body: Renzo Piano's building opened on 4 May 2023 inside Galataport, close to where the 1950s customs warehouse the museum used to occupy stood before it was pulled down — five storeys and 10,500 square metres holding exhibition halls, a cinema, a library, a design shop, a café and a restaurant, with a reflection pool five centimetres deep on the roof terrace facing the historic peninsula and the Galata Tower. Ticketed, which makes the roof an hour of looking rather than a desk. Go on a weekday morning, before the cruise ships unload onto the same quay. Galataport, Karaköy, Beyoğlu · ticketed entry

coffee-gardens|The vapur — Şehir Hatları.name: The vapur — Şehir Hatları ferry
coffee-gardens|The vapur — Şehir Hatları.teaser: The best room in Istanbul moves, and costs almost nothing.
coffee-gardens|The vapur — Şehir Hatları.body: Şirket-i Hayriye began running boats across the strait in 1851, and until the first Bosphorus bridge opened in 1973 the water was the only way over. Şehir Hatları still works 30 boats on 32 lines between 53 piers, and carried 40 million passengers in 2023. Tea comes round in tulip glasses on a tray that never spills; gulls track the stern for thrown simit. Twenty minutes, both shores lit, no table and no plug — and that is the entire point. Piers at Eminönü, Karaköy, Beşiktaş and Kadıköy · roughly 20–25 minutes across

coffee-gardens|Pierre Loti Hill.name: Pierre Loti Hill
coffee-gardens|Pierre Loti Hill.teaser: Tea above a cemetery, the whole Golden Horn laid out below.
coffee-gardens|Pierre Loti Hill.body: Louis Marie-Julien Viaud, a French naval officer who published as Pierre Loti, turned his Istanbul sojourn into the 1879 novel Aziyadé and spent his free hours on this hill; the house is now a museum under his name. A cable car climbs from the Golden Horn shore to the terrace, which sits above Eyüp cemetery — long a favoured burial ground for its closeness to the tomb of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, over which Mehmed II raised a marble tomb and a mosque after 1453. Tea and nargile, and nothing whatsoever to plug in. Eyüpsultan · cable car from the Golden Horn shore · tea and nargile

coffee-gardens|Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park.name: Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park
coffee-gardens|Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park.teaser: A sultan's private garden, two pavilions, and a glass of çay.
coffee-gardens|Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park.body: Abdülhamid II walled the outer garden of Yıldız Palace and filled it with artificial lakes, summer houses and a porcelain factory that is still going. Two of those pavilions, Çadır and Malta, now work as cafés inside what has since become a public park of some 368,000 square metres — breakfast, lunch, or a glass of tea under the trees, run by the municipal operator BELTUR along with the park's other restaurants. The climb from the Beşiktaş gate is steep enough that nobody arrives wanting to open a laptop. Yıldız Park, Beşiktaş · Çadır and Malta pavilions · public park

art|Ebru — marbling.name: Ebru — marbling
art|Ebru — marbling.teaser: Colour floated on thickened water and lifted onto paper in a single breath.
art|Ebru — marbling.body: Pigment ground from earth and mineral, cut with ox gall so it floats, dropped onto water thickened with tragacanth, combed into flowers and stones and waves, then lifted off in one sheet. UNESCO inscribed it in 2014. It was never decorative on its own terms: ebru was made for bookbinders, as endpapers, and as a ground for official documents that could not be forged twice. It lived inside the book trade, not beside it. Practised across the city; taught in Üsküdar and in Sultanahmet

art|Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil.name: Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil
art|Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil.teaser: The marbler who invented his own pattern and named it gunpowder.
art|Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil.body: Hikmet Barutçugil, born in Malatya in 1952, trained as a textile designer at the Istanbul State Academy of Fine Arts and turned to marbling in 1977. He opened Ebristan in Salacak, on the Üsküdar shore, in 1996, and works ebru onto cloth, ceramic, glass, wood and wax as well as paper. One pattern carries his name — barut ebrusu, gunpowder marbling. He teaches constantly; sessions are arranged directly rather than booked through a platform. Salacak, Üsküdar — the Asian shore facing the old city

art|Çini — the İznik blue.name: Çini — the İznik blue
art|Çini — the İznik blue.teaser: A Turkish word that means Chinese, and it is being honest.
art|Çini — the İznik blue.body: Çini is Çin — China — with an ending: Ottoman potters were chasing the prestige of imported Chinese blue-and-white, and the language kept the receipt. The İznik body is the trick, up to eighty-five per cent quartz, which is why the glaze reads as lit from behind. Production stopped in the seventeenth century and took the recipe with it. The İznik Foundation, founded in 1993 by the economist Işıl Akbaygil, reverse-engineered the quartz body and fired again from 1995. Made in İznik, Bursa province; sold and taught in Istanbul

art|Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy.name: Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy
art|Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy.teaser: Writing measured in dots, where the shape of the letter is the point.
art|Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy.body: Arabic-script calligraphy written to proportion: every letter measured in rhombic dots laid down by the same reed pen, so a hand is judged on its geometry before its content. The kit is fixed — reed pen, trimming slab, soot ink, paper sized and burnished until the ink cannot bleed. UNESCO inscribed it in 2021. Istanbul is where the Ottoman masters set the proportions the rest of the Islamic world then copied, teacher to pupil, by licence. Best seen at the Sakıp Sabancı Museum, Emirgan

art|Sakıp Sabancı Museum — the book arts.name: Sakıp Sabancı Museum — the book arts
art|Sakıp Sabancı Museum — the book arts.teaser: Five hundred years of Ottoman hands, inside a 1927 villa on the Bosphorus.
art|Sakıp Sabancı Museum — the book arts.body: The Atlı Köşk at Emirgan, built in 1927 by the Italian architect Edouard De Nari, holds what Sakıp Sabancı spent a lifetime buying: five centuries of Ottoman book arts — manuscript Qur'ans, calligraphic panels, albums, hilyes, imperial documents. It began with a single panel by Sultan Mahmud II. The family handed the house and the collection to Sabancı University in 1998 on a forty-nine-year lease, and the museum opened in 2002. This is where hüsn-i hat stops being a description. Emirgan, Sarıyer — on the European Bosphorus shore, north of Beşiktaş

art|Caferağa Medresesi.name: Caferağa Medresesi
art|Caferağa Medresesi.teaser: Sinan's medrese behind Hagia Sophia, still teaching the crafts in its cells.
art|Caferağa Medresesi.body: Mimar Sinan built this medrese for Cafer Ağa in 1559, in the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent, immediately behind Hagia Sophia.
