Since 1989 the Türk Kültürüne Hizmet Vakfı has run it as a working crafts school: ebru, hüsn-i hat, tezhip gilding, çini and ceramic, miniature, stained glass, jewellery, felt and weaving, taught in the old student cells around the courtyard. Full courses run over months; shorter sessions exist for visitors. Ask at the gate. Caferiye Sok., Sultanahmet, Fatih — immediately behind Hagia Sophia

art|Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar.name: Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar
art|Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar.teaser: Sixty-one streets named for guilds that mostly no longer trade on them.
art|Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar.body: Mehmed II began it within three years of the conquest; its stone bedesten for cloth and gems was finished by 1461, and it grew into sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops across 30,700 square metres. Every lane was a guild, and the street names are the surviving record of trades that have since left them: the main artery, Kalpakçılar Caddesi, is Hatmakers' Street, and has not sold a fur hat in living memory. It is now solid gold, end to end. Fatih · roughly Mon–Sat 09:00–19:00 · closed Sundays and religious holidays

art|Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the gold.name: Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the gold
art|Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the gold.teaser: Turks buy gold the way other countries buy government bonds.
art|Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the gold.body: This is the part of the bazaar that is not theatre. Turkish households have held savings in gold for decades because the lira keeps losing value, so the jewellers here are serving locals as much as visitors, and the price is arithmetic rather than performance: the day's gram rate, plus a workmanship charge. Ask for those two numbers separately. The conversation stops being a haggle and becomes a discussion about who made the piece. Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the bazaar's main axis, Beyazıt gate to Nuruosmaniye gate

art|Zincirli Han.name: Zincirli Han
art|Zincirli Han.teaser: The courtyard where the hammering is real and nobody chases you.
art|Zincirli Han.body: Built in 1708 on the caravanserai plan — shops below, workshops and lodgings above — and historically the han for goldsmithing and jewellery, with carpet and antique dealers alongside. It is the quietest courtyard in the bazaar and still the most working one: metal is melted and copper hammered behind the shopfronts, by ateliers that have run for generations. The master-and-apprentice chain has thinned badly. It has not broken. Go on a weekday morning and stand still. Northern end of the Grand Bazaar, Fatih · bazaar hours

art|Carpets and \"antiques\" — the hones.name: Carpets and "antiques" — the honest note
art|Carpets and \"antiques\" — the hones.teaser: If it is genuinely antique, you are not allowed to take it home.
art|Carpets and \"antiques\" — the hones.body: Turkish law protects cultural property, and genuinely old carpets, tiles, coins and icons cannot legally leave the country; dealers selling older pieces are expected to hand over museum certification that an item is not an antiquity. Which tells you precisely what the "three-hundred-year-old" rug on the wall is. A reputable seller produces that paperwork unprompted. And turn any rug over — hand-knotted backs are slightly irregular, machine-made ones suspiciously perfect. Applies anywhere in Turkey, not only inside the bazaar

art|Sahaflar Çarşısı.name: Sahaflar Çarşısı
art|Sahaflar Çarşısı.teaser: A book market on Byzantine ground, now mostly selling exam crammers.
art|Sahaflar Çarşısı.body: The booksellers' courtyard between the Grand Bazaar and Beyazıt Mosque stands on the Chartoprateia, the Byzantine paper and book market — the trade has not moved in a thousand years. Sahaf is Arabic: a dealer in written sheets. Ottoman booksellers left the Grand Bazaar for this yard in the eighteenth century; fire took it in the 1950s and it was rebuilt. Honest now — computers and then the internet hollowed the antiquarian trade out, and much of the stock is exam crammers. Between the Grand Bazaar and Beyazıt Mosque, Fatih · daily, daylight hours

art|Manol, and who actually built the ou.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
art|Manol, and who actually built the ou.name: Manol, and who actually built the oud
art|Manol, and who actually built the ou.teaser: The Turkish oud has an inventor, and his name was Manol.
art|Manol, and who actually built the ou.body: The Metropolitan Museum, which owns one of his instruments, records Emmanuel Venios — Manol — as Greek, born on Folegandros about 1838 and dead in Istanbul in 1915 or 1916; he had a workshop on İstiklal by about 1870. He is credited with the smaller, higher-tuned instrument the world now calls the Turkish oud, and his are still held to be the finest ever built. The other great maker of the tradition, Onnik Karibyan, working a generation later, was Armenian. The instrument at the centre of Turkish classical music was designed and refined by the communities this city lost. A lineage, not an address — the living trade is on Galip Dede Caddesi, Beyoğlu

art|Galip Dede Caddesi — the music stree.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
art|Galip Dede Caddesi — the music stree.name: Galip Dede Caddesi — the music street
art|Galip Dede Caddesi — the music stree.teaser: The whole instrument trade on one downhill street, the good beside the useless.
art|Galip Dede Caddesi — the music stree.body: The street falls from Tünel to the Galata Tower and has been the musicians' bazaar for decades: darbuka, davul and frame drums, bağlama and saz, ney and zurna, plus string sellers and repair benches behind the counters. The honest warning is unavoidable — a large share of the bağlamas in the windows are decorative and close to unplayable. Ask to hear one played before you think about buying. If nobody in the shop can play it, that is your answer. Galip Dede Cad., Beyoğlu — Tünel down to the Galata Tower · daytime

art|Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the n.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
art|Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the n.name: Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the names admit
art|Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the n.teaser: Four instrument names, four different empires answering at once.
art|Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the n.body: Saz is simply Persian for "instrument". Bağlama comes from bağlamak, to tie, after the gut frets tied round the neck and slid by hand — which is why the thing plays intervals a piano cannot. Kanun is Greek, kanōn, a rule or measuring rod, because the zither lays down the law of pitch that the singer and the rest of the ensemble tune to. Ud is Arabic al-ʿūd, the wood, and it is where our word lute comes from.

art|Lale Plak.group: Instruments and vinyl — the sound, made by hand
art|Lale Plak.name: Lale Plak
art|Lale Plak.teaser: Half a century at the top of the music street, run by one ear.
art|Lale Plak.body: At the Tünel end of the music street, and among the oldest record shops in the city — trading for well over fifty years, with the exact founding year disputed between sources. Hakan Atala's stock runs from Western classical and jazz, signed pressings included, to the 1970s Turkish canon: Barış Manço, Ajda Pekkan, the Anadolu rock era. It is a shop to be served in rather than to browse. Say what you are after and let him pull it. Galip Dede Cad., Tünel, Beyoğlu

around|Büyükada.name: Büyükada
around|Büyükada.teaser: The largest of the Princes' Islands, and the one where the horses were taken away.
around|Büyükada.body: Horse-drawn phaetons were the only transport on the island until 2020, when they were phased out after a serious equine disease and replaced by battery-powered electric vehicles that work like taxi cabs; islanders have since resisted the arrival of buses in the pedestrianised zone. The building everyone photographs, the Greek Orthodox orphanage on the Hristos ridge, went up in 1898 to a design by Alexander Vallaury and is believed to be the largest wooden structure in Europe and the second largest in the world — it took in children until 1964, has stood empty since, and a restoration was announced in 2021. Trotsky spent the first four years of his exile here, April 1929 to July 1933, in the Yanaros mansion, now a ruin. Şehir Hatları has run the islands 24 hours a day since 2019. The honest catch: the two buildings people travel for are both shut, the quayside kitchens are priced for day-trippers, and on a summer weekend the return-ferry queue is the memory you take home. The tell — Climb Yücetepe, the island's 202-metre high point, to the Greek Orthodox monastery of Aya Yorgi — probably founded in the tenth century, though what stands is mid-18th to 19th century — where the café on the grounds serves wine, chips and sausage sandwiches. The pilgrimage falls on 23 April, St George's Day, and the hill is mobbed for it. On the water, the 1911 Splendid Palace and its twin domes is the landmark. Adalar — 25 min by fast ferry or 40 min by regular ferry from Kabataş; also served from Eminönü, Beşiktaş, Kadıköy, Bostancı and Maltepe · Year-round; ferries run 24/7. Go on a weekday out of high summer.

around|Heybeliada.name: Heybeliada
around|Heybeliada.teaser: The quiet island next door, with a seminary at the top of it that has been closed since 1971 and is still a diplomatic file.
around|Heybeliada.body: The Theological School of Halki was founded in 1844 inside the Hagia Triada monastery and trained clergy for the Ecumenical Patriarchate until 1971, when the Constitutional Court struck down parts of Turkey's private higher-education law; it has never reopened and remains closed to the public. The Naval High School overlooking the jetty was founded in 1773 and holds the Byzantine church of the Kamariotissa and the relocated grave of Edward Barton, Elizabeth I's ambassador to the Porte. The island is 2.35 square kilometres with 4,424 residents at the 2022 count, rising to around 30,000 in high summer. Phaetons were banned here in 2020 along with the rest of the islands and replaced by electric vehicles; private cars are still prohibited, with only ambulances, fire tenders and police allowed. The catch: both buildings that give the island its meaning are institutional and shut, so come for the pine ridge and the swimming, not for a tour. The tell — Hire a bike at the jetty and ride the ring road under the pines — the island is small enough to circle in an hour and quiet enough that you hear it. Aya Triada on Ümit Tepesi, restored by Patriarch Photios I in the ninth century, is the roofline you look up at from the road, and looking up is as close as you get. Adalar — the call before Büyükada on ferries from Kabataş, Eminönü, Beşiktaş, Kadıköy, Bostancı and Maltepe · Year-round; the island empties out of season, which is the point.

around|Anadolu Kavağı & Yoros Kalesi.name: Anadolu Kavağı & Yoros Kalesi
around|Anadolu Kavağı & Yoros Kalesi.teaser: The last village before the Black Sea, and the much-conquered castle on the hill above it.
around|Anadolu Kavağı & Yoros Kalesi.body: Yoros stands above the confluence of the Bosphorus and the Black Sea and changed hands more often than almost any fort in Turkey: the Ottomans took it in 1305 and held it again from 1391 to 1414, the Genoese held it for the forty years to 1454 — which is why locals still call it the Genoese Castle — and Mehmed II refortified it after 1453. It was excavated between 2018 and 2021 and is open to the public again, though the ground immediately around it remains a military area and is closed; the site sits on the UNESCO tentative list. The village below is tiny, 1,517 residents at the 2022 count plus the garrisons, and keeps a mosque commissioned by Ali Pasha of Midilli in 1593 and a fountain of 1785. The catch: the entire quay is calibrated to a boat that arrives and leaves, the layover is fixed, and missing the return sailing puts you on a long bus down the Asian shore. The tell — Fish on the quay — pick it off the ice and agree the price before it is cooked, because this is a captive-audience waterfront and the bill is where day-trippers get caught. Then walk up to the castle: a steep twenty minutes from the pier, with the Third Bosphorus Bridge on one side and open Black Sea on the other. Beykoz — terminus of Şehir Hatları's twice-daily Long Bosphorus Tour from Eminönü, calling at Sarıyer and Rumeli Kavağı on the way up · The long tour runs twice daily; confirm the timetable with Şehir Hatları on the day of travel.

around|Rumeli Kavağı.name: Rumeli Kavağı
around|Rumeli Kavağı.teaser: Get off one stop early, on the European bank, where the fish is the same water and the audience is not.
around|Rumeli Kavağı.body: This is the northernmost settlement on the European side of the strait, and the majority of its 3,560 residents (2024 count) descend from Eastern Black Sea migration — which is what ends up on the plate. The village is known locally for exactly three things: fish, mussels and figs. A Byzantine fortress once stood here and was demolished on Mehmed II's order; excavation has also turned up traces of a Byzantine temple and harbour works beneath the settlement. The catch: nearly every cruise passenger stays aboard for the castle across the water, so there are fewer kitchens open here and no schedule built around visitors — check before you commit an evening to it. The tell — Midye — mussels — and whatever came in that morning, cooked plainly and without ceremony. If you want open sea rather than strait, the Rumeli Feneri lighthouse and the fishing hamlet of Garipçe are a short ride further north. Sarıyer — the last European call on the Long Bosphorus Tour, one stop before Anadolu Kavağı · Best in the fish months, autumn through early spring.

around|Hıdiv Kasrı.name: Hıdiv Kasrı
around|Hıdiv Kasrı.teaser: An Art Nouveau summer palace built in 1907 for the Khedive of Egypt, on a bluff over the Bosphorus.
around|Hıdiv Kasrı.body: The Khedive of Egypt — the Ottoman viceroy of a province richer than most of the empire — built his holiday house on this headland in 1907, and it is one of the very few grand houses around Istanbul where you get inside the rooms rather than photographing a façade, because the building now trades as a restaurant and café inside its own public park. The catch is twofold. It is a working hospitality business in a historic shell, so go for the terrace and the grounds rather than for the cooking. And I could not reach a live source to confirm current opening hours in August 2026 — treat the visit as unconfirmed and telephone before you make the climb, which is a genuine hill from the waterline and unpleasant in high summer. The tell — The park and the terrace over the strait, best in the morning before the light goes flat. A drink is what buys you the interior, so order one and walk the rooms rather than booking a full dinner. Beykoz — Çubuklu, on the Asian shore; ferry to Kanlıca then a climb, or bus and taxi from Beykoz · Not verified for 2026 — call ahead before travelling. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

around|Polonezköy.name: Polonezköy
around|Polonezköy.teaser: A Polish village in the Beykoz forest, founded in 1842 by an exiled prince and still holding on to the language.
around|Polonezköy.body: Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski established the settlement in 1842 for Poles displaced by the failed November Uprising and named it Adampol, a Polish rendering of the Turkish Adamköy; it started with twelve inhabitants and grew through later waves of emigration. Many went home after Poland regained independence in 1918, and those who stayed took Turkish citizenship in 1938. At the 2022 count the village had 346 residents, of whom roughly ninety speak fluent Polish — so what survives is a community held together by memory, a church and a summer festival of Polish folk bands, not a living Polish town. The catch: at weekends Istanbul drives out here en masse and the single approach road becomes a queue. Go midweek or do not go. The tell — The Memorial House of Zofia Rizi, which keeps the photographs, books, documents and original interiors of a village house; the church of Our Lady of Częstochowa; and the Polish cemetery, where 92 graves have been restored. The pensions along the road serve the long forest-edge breakfast that is the actual reason most Istanbullus make the drive. Beykoz — about 30 km from the historic centre; realistically a drive or a taxi, there is no useful public transport · Weekdays. The summer festival is the one weekend worth the traffic.

around|Belgrad Ormanı.group: Forest, coast and the far shore
around|Belgrad Ormanı.name: Belgrad Ormanı
around|Belgrad Ormanı.teaser: Five and a half thousand hectares of forest with Istanbul's Ottoman waterworks buried in it.
around|Belgrad Ormanı.body: The forest takes its name from the Serbs deported here after Süleyman the Magnificent's 1521 siege of Belgrade, settled to maintain the water supply. Two Ottoman systems ran through it: the older Kırkçeşme network, rebuilt by Mimar Sinan under Süleyman, and the eighteenth-century Taksim system, whose Mahmud I aqueduct went up at Bahçeköy in 1732. What you actually walk to are the bents — the dammed Ottoman reservoirs — on a 6.5-kilometre marked track that starts at Neşet Suyu, with seven picnic grounds of which Büyük Bent is the busiest. The catch, and it sends people to the wrong district: Mağlova, Sinan's masterpiece and the aqueduct in every photograph, is not in this forest. It stands in the Alibey valley near Cebeci in Sultangazi, 257 metres long and 35 metres high on two tiers, built between 1555 and 1562 — and roughly a quarter of it is drowned by the Alibeyköy reservoir, so the full span is visible only when the water level drops. The tell — Start at Bahçeköy, walk the Neşet Suyu track to Büyük Bent, and detour to the Atatürk Arboretum — over 2,000 plant species, about twenty minutes on foot from the village. Bring the food with you: this is picnic country, not restaurant country, and Bahçeköy is where you buy it before you go in. Sarıyer and Eyüp — 5,524 hectares; Bahçeköy is the hub and is well served by city buses, roughly an hour from Beyoğlu depending on traffic · Autumn for colour, spring for water. Picnic areas fill on summer weekends.

around|Şile & Ağva.group: Forest, coast and the far shore
around|Şile & Ağva.name: Şile & Ağva
around|Şile & Ağva.teaser: Istanbul's Black Sea coast: an 1859 French-built lighthouse, a crimped cotton cloth, and a village between two rivers.
around|Şile & Ağva.body: The Şile lighthouse was built in 1859 by French engineers for Sultan Abdülmecid I and lit in 1860 — a 19-metre octagonal tower carrying eight 925-millimetre catadioptric lenses with a range of 20 nautical miles, electrified since 1968 and open to visitors as a historic site. The town also gives its name to Şile bezi, the crimped cotton cloth sold across Istanbul's bazaars, with a fair for it each summer; the fourteenth-century Genoese castle on Ocaklı Ada was renovated in 2015 to widespread mockery for looking like a cartoon. Ağva sits between the Göksu and the Yeşilçay — the name means 'between the rivers' — with a 2.5-kilometre beach and small boats running up the Göksu, and its 2,150 residents swell to around 15,000 in season. The catch here is not crowds, it is water: the undercurrents on this coast are strong enough that people drown at these beaches every year. Swim between flags or not at all. The tell — Walk into the lighthouse — one of very few in Turkey you can enter. Buy the Şile bezi in Şile rather than off a Sultanahmet stall. And in Ağva take the river rather than the sea: the pensions face the Göksu, which is the argument for staying the night instead of driving 97 km twice in a day. Şile district — Şile is the northernmost point of Istanbul province; Ağva is 38 km further east, about 97 km from the centre · June to September for swimming; the coast road jams every summer weekend.

around|Yalova Termal.group: Forest, coast and the far shore
around|Yalova Termal.name: Yalova Termal
around|Yalova Termal.teaser: Seventy minutes across the Marmara to springs the Byzantines bathed in, and a mansion that was moved to spare a tree.
around|Yalova Termal.body: The springs at Termal, inland from the port, have been in use since Byzantine times; Evliya Çelebi recorded the Kurşunlu Banyo, the Leaded Bath, in the seventeenth century, and the complex was enlarged under Abdülhamid II and again in the Republic's first decades. Down at Yalova stands the Yürüyen Köşk, the Walking Mansion: built between 21 August and 12 September 1929, it was found the following summer to be having its roof damaged by the branches of an old plane tree, and Atatürk ordered the building moved rather than the tree cut. Railway track was laid beneath the foundations, the terrace was shifted on 8 August 1930 and the main house on 10 August — about five metres east — under Istanbul's chief engineer Ali Galip Alnar and public works director Yusuf Ziya Erdem. It was restored in 2006 and is a museum today. The tell — The Kurşunlu Banyo for the bath and the Walking Mansion for the story — but these are two separate stops, not one trip. The mansion sits in the grounds of the horticultural research institute at Yalova, while the baths are up the valley at Termal, so budget a dolmuş or taxi between them, and check the last ferry back before you undress. Yalova, south across the Sea of Marmara — 70 min from Yenikapı by fast ferry, 45 min from Pendik, about 40 min by seabus from Bostancı and Kartal · Year-round; the baths are better in cold weather.

around|Bandırma.group: Forest, coast and the far shore
around|Bandırma.name: Bandırma
around|Bandırma.teaser: Two hours across the Marmara to the railhead — the route to İzmir that is not a plane.
around|Bandırma.body: This is the crossing rather than the destination. From Bandırma two TCDD trains a day run down to İzmir, the 6 Eylül Ekspresi and the 17 Eylül Ekspresi, which makes ferry-and-train the old civilised way between Turkey's two biggest coastal cities. South of the town lies Lake Kuş — Manyas, 'Bird Paradise' — 24,047 hectares, a national park since 1959, added to the Ramsar list in 1998, with 239 recorded bird species. The catch is real: I could not load İDO's live timetable to confirm current sailings, sailings on this line are limited rather than frequent, and vehicle rules differ by hull type, with LPG and CNG cars restricted on some boats. Confirm both the sailing and the train connection before you commit, because missing the boat here means a very long bus. The tell — Go for the bird lake or for the onward train, not for Bandırma itself, which is a working port and does not pretend otherwise. If you are making the İzmir run, book the ferry and the express as one plan and re-check both on the morning of travel. Bandırma, on the south shore of the Sea of Marmara — İDO fast ferry from Yenikapı, about 120 minutes, with a seabus interchange from Bostancı · Sailings limited and seasonal — verify with İDO before travelling. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

provisioning|Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Gü.group: The markets and the streets behind them
provisioning|Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Gü.name: Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Güneşlibahçe Sokağı
provisioning|Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Gü.teaser: Five minutes uphill from the ferry: the fish row, the butchers and the greengrocers that feed Kadıköy's own kitchens.
provisioning|Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Gü.body: The market is not a building, it is a grid of short streets behind Söğütlüçeşme, and Güneşlibahçe Sokağı is its spine — OpenStreetMap maps fishmongers at nos. 1–3, a greengrocer at no. 9, butchers, bakeries and a spice counter inside about eighty metres of each other, with more fish and a butcher's row round the corner on Serasker Caddesi. Buy to the Turkish fishing calendar rather than to a shopping list: commercial fishing runs 1 September to 15 April, so palamut lands from September, lüfer through the autumn and hamsi from late autumn into winter, while between mid-April and the end of August almost everything on ice is farmed levrek and çipura or flown in. Fish is chalked per kilo and cleaned at the counter at no charge; produce is priced per kilo too, and the crates behind the stall are usually cheaper than the display. Stall names on this street turn over faster than the trades do, so shop the counter, not the sign — verify any single shop before you make a special trip for it. The tell — Whole palamut in autumn, gutted and scaled at the counter; ripe tomatoes and a bunch of flat parsley from the greengrocer at Güneşlibahçe 9; then the butchers' row for kuzu pirzola. Say "temizlensin" for the fish to be cleaned. Güneşlibahçe Sokağı and Serasker Caddesi, Osmanağa, Kadıköy · Stalls set their own hours; the street trades daytime and is busiest late morning. Verify per shop.

provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.group: The markets and the streets behind them
provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.name: Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice Bazaar, and what it is now
provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.teaser: Eighty-five shops under a 1660 vault, and fewer of them sell spice every year.
provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.body: Turhan Hatice Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, commissioned the hall as the revenue arm of the Yeni Cami complex; the court architect Koca Kasım Ağa drew it and it was going up in the last months of 1660, after the Great Fire. There are 85 shops today, and the honest reading is that spice is retreating from them: pre-boxed lokum, pistachio pyramids built for photographs, saffron sold by the gram to people who will never cook with it. One measure of the drift — the Ucuzcular spice house, whose family dates its trade to 1886 and which traded under that name for generations, now runs as Hayfene, sells chiefly online, and states on its own contact page that there is no counter sale at its premises. Treat the hall as architecture and orientation, then walk out of the back gate and buy on Hasırcılar Caddesi. The tell — If you do buy inside, buy only weighable single things you can smell first — Urfa isot, Antep pul biber, dried mint, sumac — and refuse anything pre-boxed with a photograph on the lid. Never accept the first price on saffron. Rüstempaşa Mahallesi, Eminönü, Fatih · Recorded in OpenStreetMap as Mon–Sat 08:00–19:00, Sun 09:30–19:00; individual shops vary.

provisioning|Hasırcılar Caddesi — the wo.group: The markets and the streets behind them
provisioning|Hasırcılar Caddesi — the wo.name: Hasırcılar Caddesi — the working street
provisioning|Hasırcılar Caddesi — the wo.teaser: The street the bazaar's own traders shop on, running west from the Spice Bazaar's back gate.
provisioning|Hasırcılar Caddesi — the wo.body: Hasırcılar is where the wholesale rhythm survives: coffee roasters, nut and dried-fruit merchants, cheese, pickle and pulse counters, and a fishmonger — OpenStreetMap maps the roaster Kurukahveci Nuri Toplar and the fish counter Taze Balıkçı directly on it, a hundred metres from the bazaar's tourist trade. Quantities here are assumed in kilos rather than gift boxes, prices are lower than inside the hall for the same goods, and nobody presses a sample on you to start a negotiation. The street works on the same clock as the wholesalers: weekday mornings, while the handcarts are still moving, and many counters are shut on Sunday. This is the buy for bulk pul biber, isot, nar ekşisi, pulses, walnuts and grating cheese. The tell — Ask by weight and in Turkish units — "yarım kilo" for half a kilo, "çeyrek" for a quarter. Taste kaşar before it is cut, and buy pepper flakes here rather than in the hall. Hasırcılar Caddesi, Rüstempaşa, Eminönü, Fatih · Daytime, weekdays busiest; most counters shut by early evening and many close Sunday. Verify per shop.

provisioning|Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı.group: The markets and the streets behind them
provisioning|Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı.name: Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı
provisioning|Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı.teaser: The European side's working fish market, wedged into the çarşı two minutes from the ferry.
provisioning|Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı.body: Beşiktaş keeps its fish trade in the covered block behind the square, mapped in OpenStreetMap as Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı, and unlike the Beyoğlu row it is still a market before it is a restaurant: whole fish on ice, chalked per kilo, gutted and scaled at the counter for nothing. For anyone provisioning off a Bosphorus berth this is the nearest serious fish counter on the European shore — the argument for it over Kadıköy is simply that you do not cross the water with a cold box. The çarşı around it closes the rest of the list inside a hundred metres: nut and dried-fruit counters, helva makers, a tea seller, greengrocers. Hours are not published for the block, so treat it as a daytime market and go mid-morning. The tell — Learn the lüfer ladder before you buy — çinekop, sarıkanat, lüfer and kofana are one fish at four ages, and Turkey enforces a minimum landing size, so a stall offering you the smallest grade is telling you something about itself. Ask for "temizlensin" and say whether you want it scaled. Beşiktaş çarşı, behind Beşiktaş Meydanı, Beşiktaş · Not published; trades daytime, busiest mid-morning. Verify before a special trip.

provisioning|Salı Pazarı and the weekly.group: The markets and the streets behind them
provisioning|Salı Pazarı and the weekly.name: Salı Pazarı and the weekly pazar circuit
provisioning|Salı Pazarı and the weekly.teaser: Istanbul's Tuesday market is Kadıköy's, not Beşiktaş's — and it has moved from where its name suggests.
provisioning|Salı Pazarı and the weekly.body: Worth correcting before you plan a week around it. The Salı Pazarı that Istanbul cooks mean is Kadıköy's, and it no longer stands where the name is remembered: the İSPARK car park on the old ground is still signed Eski Salı Pazarı Otoparkı, while the market itself is mapped up at Hasanpaşa, out towards Kurbağalıdere. Beşiktaş's own weekly street pazar is recorded in OpenStreetMap as a Saturday market, 08:00–20:00, on the ground north-west of Beşiktaş Meydanı, and Bomonti's semt pazarı runs most days with Wednesday off — so the circuit is Tuesday east, Saturday west. The pazar is where price is settled: produce goes for a fraction of shop money, sold by the crate and the kilo, and the last hour before the trestles come down is when growers cut rather than cart it home. The tell — Buy what a shop sells badly and a pazar sells brilliantly: crates of tomatoes for sauce, herbs by the armful, green almonds and unripe plums in spring, quince and pomegranate in autumn. Bring your own bags and small notes — cards are not taken. Salı Pazarı, Hasanpaşa, Kadıköy; Beşiktaş pazarı, north-west of Beşiktaş Meydanı; Bomonti Semt Pazarı, Gökkuşağı Sokağı 6, Şişli · Kadıköy: Tuesday. Beşiktaş: Saturday 08:00–20:00. Bomonti: 09:00–19:30, closed Wednesday (all OpenStreetMap). Confirm the week locally.

provisioning|Kadınlar Pazarı.group: The markets and the streets behind them
provisioning|Kadınlar Pazarı.name: Kadınlar Pazarı
provisioning|Kadınlar Pazarı.teaser: The Siirt quarter's larder, trading under the Valens Aqueduct at Zeyrek.
provisioning|Kadınlar Pazarı.body: This is a community market rather than a general one: the streets around it were settled by families from Siirt and the south-east, and the shops carry what that kitchen needs — otlu peynir threaded with wild herbs, thick pistachios, isot, comb honey, dried pulses — alongside the büryan ocakları where lamb hangs in pit ovens cut into the floor. OpenStreetMap records unusually long trading here, roughly 08:00–22:00 Wednesday to Saturday, 08:00–23:00 on Sunday and from 09:00 Monday and Tuesday, which makes it the one provisioning stop on the historic peninsula still working after the bazaar quarters have shuttered for the evening. It sits west of the Spice Bazaar, below the aqueduct arches at Zeyrek — uphill, and worth the walk for the cheese alone. Individual shops keep their own hours inside those bounds. The tell — Buy otlu peynir by the piece and only after tasting: the herb should read as wild garlic and thyme, not as salt carrying a green fleck. Then isot, Siirt pistachios, and a slab of comb honey. Kadınlar Pazarı, Zeyrek, Fatih · Wed–Sat 08:00–22:00; Sun 08:00–23:00; Mon–Tue 09:00–22:00 (OpenStreetMap). Shops vary.

provisioning|Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi.name: Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi
provisioning|Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi.teaser: One counter on Tahmis Sokak that has ground the city's coffee since 1871.
provisioning|Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi.body: The house is in its 155th year — its own site runs the anniversary as "155. YIL" and its official channel carries the founding date in the handle — and it is still at Tahmis Sokağı 66, in the purpose-built block the company credits to the architect Zühtü Başar. There are only three shops in the whole city, all confirmed on the company's own contact pages: the Eminönü merkez, a Sirkeci branch, and Kadıköy at Osmanağa Mahallesi, Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12 — anything sold as Mehmet Efendi anywhere else is retail packaging, not the counter grind. The queue is long, moves fast, and almost everyone in it buys the same thing: Türk kahvesi ground to order and handed over still warm. The company does not publish shop hours on its own site, which is worth knowing before you cross the Golden Horn for it. The tell — Buy Türk kahvesi ground fresh at the counter, in the smallest pack you will finish within a fortnight — it is milled far finer than espresso and roasted for cezve extraction, so it will choke a portafilter basket. Tahmis Sokağı 66, Eminönü 34116, İstanbul (branch: Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12, Kadıköy 34714) · Not published on the company's own site — confirm before a special trip.

provisioning|Namlı Gurme.name: Namlı Gurme
provisioning|Namlı Gurme.teaser: One Karaköy counter covering pastırma, cheese, olives, oil, honey and tahin — open seven days a week from seven in the morning.
provisioning|Namlı Gurme.body: This is the single most efficient provisioning stop on the European side, and its own shop publishes the numbers, VAT included: çemeni sıyrılmış pastırma, the fenugreek crust scraped back, ₺5,400/kg; an 850 g kangal sucuk made from 100% beef in the house's own workshop, ₺1,836; Gelibolu eski kaşar ₺1,690/kg and Kars Göle eski kaşar ₺1,080/kg; Erzincan tulum ₺1,180/kg, Van otlu peynir ₺1,490/kg, Ezine beyaz peynir ₺598 a block, Balıkesir buffalo butter ₺576 for 450 g. On the dry side: kuru sele olives ₺780/kg, Ayvalık kırma yeşil ₺590/kg, a litre of Makaron olive oil ₺1,080, 330 g of tahin ₺240, Elazığ mulberry pekmez ₺350 and nar ekşisi ₺350 for 350 ml. Honey is the outlier — Hakkari karakovan comb honey ₺4,200 — and these are the online-store figures checked in August 2026, so the counter can differ. The hours are the real advantage: Monday to Sunday, 07:00 to 22:00. The tell — Pastırma cut to order in front of you, thin enough to read through — ask for the çemeni sıyrılmış if you want the meat rather than the fenugreek. Kangal sucuk whole, not sliced. A kilo of Gelibolu eski kaşar for grating, and tulum for the meze board. Kemankeş Mahallesi, Mumhane Caddesi, Atilla İş Hanı No: 6/A, Karaköy, Beyoğlu · Monday–Sunday 07:00–22:00 (the shop's own listing)

provisioning|Reşat Balık.name: Reşat Balık
provisioning|Reşat Balık.teaser: A fishmonger in the Beyoğlu fish market since 1941 — and one of the few that opens on Sunday.
provisioning|Reşat Balık.body: The house dates itself to 1941 on its own site and runs two counters: Sahne Sokak No: 8 inside the Balık Pazarı off İstiklal, and Bağdat Caddesi No: 476/c at Bostancı on the Asian side. OpenStreetMap records the Beyoğlu shop as Mon–Sat 08:00–20:00 and Sun 08:00–19:00, which matters — most Istanbul fish counters are done by Sunday lunchtime. Be clear-eyed about the setting: the Beyoğlu fish market around it has thinned into meyhane tables and souvenir stalls, so the row is now more restaurant than market and the fish counter is the reason to walk in, not the atmosphere. It is the closest serious fishmonger to Pera and Galata, which is the practical case for it. The tell — Buy to the calendar. Palamut from September, lüfer through the autumn, hamsi from late autumn into winter; Turkish commercial fishing closes 15 April to 1 September, so anything glossy in July is farmed or flown. Have it cleaned at the counter — "temizlensin". Sahne Sokak No: 8, Balık Pazarı, Beyoğlu (also Bağdat Caddesi No: 476/c, Bostancı) · Mon–Sat 08:00–20:00, Sun 08:00–19:00 (OpenStreetMap)

provisioning|Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar.name: Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar
provisioning|Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar.teaser: A Saturday producers' market where the residue analyses are on a desk you can walk up to and read.
provisioning|Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar.body: The %100 Ekolojik Pazarlar network lists a Şişli market on Saturday, alongside Bakırköy on Friday and Kartal on Sunday, and describes the model in its own words as a "halk pazarı" — a public market where growers sell direct, not a boutique with a certificate on the wall. Certification is backed by field visits and laboratory analyses, and the market keeps a public-relations stall where the inspection reports and residue results for what is on sale can be read on the spot. This is the practical source for the things a city shop handles worst: raw honey, farm eggs, small-dairy cheeses and butter, cold-pressed oils, unsprayed greens. The covered ground is mapped in OpenStreetMap as Bomonti Semt Pazarı at Gökkuşağı Sokağı 6 — the same yard that hosts the Sunday antiques market, so check which day you are walking into. The tell — Ask a stallholder for the analiz raporu; the straight ones point you at the results desk rather than talking about it. Buy honey, eggs, butter and leaves here — not staples, which are cheaper at a semt pazarı. Feriköy covered market ground, Gökkuşağı Sokağı 6, Şişli · Saturday (operator's own listing). Times not published — go in the morning.

provisioning|Matbah-ı Âmire — the imperi.name: Matbah-ı Âmire — the imperial kitchens
provisioning|Matbah-ı Âmire — the imperi.teaser: Eight hundred cooks, four thousand fed daily — and the restraint you still taste.
provisioning|Matbah-ı Âmire — the imperi.body: The Topkapı kitchens employed more than 800 people and cooked for roughly 4,000 a day. Fire took them in 1574 and Mimar Sinan rebuilt them: ten domed buildings, two rows of twenty wide chimneys. That scale bred a style — measured spicing, rice over bulgur, vegetables cooked in olive oil and eaten cold — which is still what Istanbul means when it calls a dish its own rather than Anatolia's. The rooms now hold 10,700 pieces of Chinese porcelain. WHERE Topkapı Palace, Sultanahmet · the kitchens run down one side of the second courtyard

provisioning|The ocakbaşı.name: The ocakbaşı
provisioning|The ocakbaşı.teaser: A bar with a charcoal trench in it, and you sit at the trench.
provisioning|The ocakbaşı.body: Not an Istanbul invention. The fire counter came up with twentieth-century migration from the south-east and naturalised so completely that visitors now read it as the city's own night food. The order is fixed: liver first, then the skewers, then a lahmacun to close, and the rakı does not stop. A handful of new rooms are reworking the form this year — shorter menus, real wine lists, the same trench. Sit where the smoke goes. Arnavutköy, Gümüşsuyu and Sarıyer hold the new wave; Kadıköy holds the old

provisioning|The meyhane table.name: The meyhane table
provisioning|The meyhane table.teaser: Cold mezes, then hot, then fish — a drinking licence that was never Muslim.
provisioning|The meyhane table.body: Alcohol was forbidden to Muslims, so the keeping of a drinking house fell in practice almost entirely to Greeks, Armenians and Jews. That is why the meyhane looks as it does: the long table of cold mezes before the hot, rakı cut with water until it turns white, fasıl players moving between tables. The wealth tax of 1942, the pogrom of September 1955 and the measures of 1964 removed the authors. The form stayed. Asmalımescit and Nevizade in Beyoğlu; Balat and Kadıköy for the quieter version

provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.group: Two markets, and how to eat standing up in them
provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.name: Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice Bazaar
provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.teaser: Built to fund a mosque, named after the province that paid for it.
provisioning|Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice B.body: Commissioned by Hatice Turhan Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, and begun in the last months of 1660 after the great fire of that July. It was the arasta of the New Mosque complex: eighty-five shops whose rent maintained the mosque. The name is Egypt — the building went up on revenues from the Ottoman province, and much of what filled it arrived by the same route. Walk the L, buy nothing, and eat in the streets behind it where the traders do. WHERE Eminönü, beside the New Mosque · the lanes off Hasırcılar Çarşısı are where to eat

provisioning|Kadıköy market streets.group: Two markets, and how to eat standing up in them
provisioning|Kadıköy market streets.name: Kadıköy market streets
provisioning|Kadıköy market streets.teaser: Chalcedon, the settlement Byzantium's founders were told only the blind would have chosen.
provisioning|Kadıköy market streets.body: Megarian Greeks settled here in 685 BC, a generation before Byzantium; the oracle's line about a capital built opposite the city of the blind is a joke at Chalcedon's expense that has outlasted the city. The Turkish name means village of the judge, for Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first kadı after 1453. Today it is a few sloping lanes of fishmongers, picklers and cheese counters, and the correct way through is to eat at every second stall. WHERE Güneşlibahçe Sokak and the lanes around it, Caferağa · ferry from Karaköy or Eminönü

provisioning|Simit.name: Simit
provisioning|Simit.teaser: Made in this city since 1525, and still carried through it on a tray.
provisioning|Simit.body: Archival records put simit production in Istanbul at 1525, with weight and price fixed at Üsküdar in 1593 — a regulated staple, not a snack. Evliya Çelebi counted seventy simit bakeries in the 1630s. The word comes from the Arabic for fine flour. Dipped in grape molasses and rolled in sesame before baking, it is chewy hot and cardboard cold, so buy from a tray that is moving. Throwing pieces to the gulls off the ferry is not a tourist habit. Every ferry pier and street corner · the carts at the Kadıköy and Karaköy landings turn over fastest

provisioning|Balık ekmek.name: Balık ekmek
provisioning|Balık ekmek.teaser: Grilled mackerel in bread — and the famous boats are the version to skip.
provisioning|Balık ekmek.body: A fillet of oily fish, usually mackerel, grilled and put in a bun with onion and leaves, and it is the city's signature thing eaten standing up. The painted boats at Eminönü serve it off the water and are the image on every postcard; they are also an industrialised operation aimed squarely at visitors. Cross to the Karaköy or Kadıköy side and buy from a counter with a queue of people on their way to work. Avoid Eminönü square · the Karaköy fish market and the Kadıköy pier end are the working versions

provisioning|Midye dolma.name: Midye dolma
provisioning|Midye dolma.teaser: Rice-stuffed mussels counted out one at a time, lemon squeezed over the shell.
provisioning|Midye dolma.body: The earliest Istanbul record of it is Armenian — an 1888 account describes Armenian cooks preparing large mussels with sheep's-tail fat. The filling is rice with currants, black pepper and red pepper; the lemon is not garnish but the thing that stops the rice drying out. Since the 1960s the carts have been run largely by families from Mardin, whose version runs hotter. You eat until you stop, then you pay for the shells. Kadıköy's bar streets and Beyoğlu after midnight · the trays appear when the bars fill

provisioning|Kokoreç.name: Kokoreç
provisioning|Kokoreç.teaser: Lamb intestine wound round offal over charcoal, chopped into bread with oregano.
provisioning|Kokoreç.body: Suckling-lamb intestine wrapped around sweetbread, heart and kidney, turned on a horizontal spit and basted with lemon and oil, then chopped fine and packed into half a baguette. The word entered Turkish in 1920, in a short story that described it as a Greek dish; the name goes back to South Slavic, though whether Greek took it via Albanian or the two borrowed it separately is disputed. When EU accession was live in the early 2000s the Turkish press argued about whether Brussels would ban it. Beyoğlu's back streets and the Kadıköy bar quarter, from midnight

provisioning|Baklava.group: The counters that outlived the empire
provisioning|Baklava.name: Baklava
provisioning|Baklava.teaser: Handed to the Janissaries on the fifteenth of Ramadan; claimed by four cuisines since.
provisioning|Baklava.body: The one hard Ottoman fact is a ceremony: on the fifteenth of Ramadan the Sultan sent trays of baklava down to the Janissary barracks in a procession called the Baklava Alayı. The origins are genuinely unsettled — Byzantine koptoplakous, Central Asian Turkic layered breads and the Arab lauzinaj of tenth-century cookbooks all have serious advocates. What is settled is the name: since 2013 Gaziantep Baklavası has carried an EU protected geographical indication. Sold citywide · the counters worth the walk are the ones with an oven behind the display

provisioning|Pastırma and sucuk.group: The counters that outlived the empire
provisioning|Pastırma and sucuk.name: Pastırma and sucuk
provisioning|Pastırma and sucuk.teaser: Air-dried beef under a fenugreek crust — and the word pastrami came from.
provisioning|Pastırma and sucuk.body: Pastırma comes from bastırma, to press. The Ottomans took a Byzantine cured beef called paston and renamed it; Kayseri became the centre, and an 1893 British Foreign Office report already singled the city out for it. The crust is çemen — crushed fenugreek, cumin, garlic and hot paprika — over meat dried hard. Sucuk is its sausage cousin, garlic-heavy, fried for breakfast. English took pastrami by way of Yiddish, perhaps crossed with salami. The cured-meat shops sit along the streets flanking the Spice Bazaar in Eminönü

provisioning|Lokum.group: The counters that outlived the empire
provisioning|Lokum.name: Lokum
provisioning|Lokum.teaser: Starch, sugar and rosewater — and a founding date historians will not sign off.
provisioning|Lokum.body: The house of Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir dates its Bahçekapı shop to 1777, when its founder came down from Kastamonu; the Oxford Companion to Food notes there is no real evidence for the invention claim, and Tim Richardson has written on how often confectionery dates are commercial rather than historical. The sweet itself is a gel of starch and sugar scented with rosewater, mastic, bergamot or lemon, sometimes loaded with pistachio or walnut. Buy it cut from the tray. WHERE Bahçekapı, Eminönü · a short walk from the Spice Bazaar

street-food|Karaköy Güllüoğlu.name: Karaköy Güllüoğlu
street-food|Karaköy Güllüoğlu.teaser: One counter in Karaköy, open past midnight, run by the fifth generation of the family that made Gaziantep a baklava town.
street-food|Karaköy Güllüoğlu.body: The dynasty's origin is documented outside the family's own marketing: baklava was introduced to Gaziantep in 1871 by Çelebi Güllü, who had learned the recipe from a Syrian chef in Damascus. The city's version was registered as a Turkish geographical indication in 2008 and became Antep Baklavası, a Protected Geographical Indication under the European Commission, in 2013 — the first Turkish product to receive one. This house dates itself to 1843 and puts Nadir Güllü at the counter as "the fifth generation representative of a family that has been making baklava since 1843," trained by his father and master Hacı Mustafa Güllü. The decisive fact is the smallest one: their contact page lists a single shop, Kemankeş Caddesi 67, and OpenStreetMap records the same telephone the house publishes, +90 850 308 45 45, against hours running to one in the morning. The tell — Fıstıklı kuru baklava — the dry pistachio one, no cream, cut small and stacked; it is the version that survives being carried onto a boat. Ask by weight (porsiyon or half a kilo), not by the piece. The tell for the whole city is here: Karaköy Güllüoğlu has one shop, and it is in Karaköy. A Güllüoğlu sign anywhere else is a different branch of the family. Kemankeş Karamustafa Paşa Mah., Kemankeş Cad. No:67, 34425 Karaköy — Beyoğlu · Mon–Sat 07:30–01:00, Sun 08:00–01:00 (OpenStreetMap; the house publishes only a 19:00 courier cut-off)

street-food|Faruk Güllü.name: Faruk Güllü
street-food|Faruk Güllü.teaser: The counter-lesson: the largest holder of the Güllüoğlu name has quietly stopped putting it on the door.
street-food|Faruk Güllü.body: Followed by hand on 15 August 2026: gulluoglu.com.tr answers with a 301 to farukgulluoglu.com.tr, which answers with a second 301 to farukgullu.com.tr. The shopfront brand is now "Faruk Güllü Baklava" while the copyright line on that same page still reads "Baklavacı Güllüoğlu Gıda Sanayi ve Dış Ticaret A.Ş." — the company kept the old name, the sign dropped it. The operating address given is a plant on Fırat Plastik Caddesi in Büyükçekmece, an industrial estate at the far western edge of the city, not a shop in the old town. Güllü is a large family and several descendants trade under names built from it; the surname is inherited, the kitchen is not. The tell — Read the first name, not the surname. Nadir Güllü means the single Karaköy shop. Faruk means this operation, which sells through many branches and now leads with the given name. If a Güllüoğlu counter is inside a shopping centre or an airport, it is neither of the two above. That is not a verdict on the pastry — it is a warning against assuming you are eating what you read about. Türkoba Mah., Fırat Plastik Cad. No:35, Büyükçekmece — head office, not a shop

street-food|Hafız Mustafa 1864.name: Hafız Mustafa 1864
street-food|Hafız Mustafa 1864.teaser: A Bahçekapı sugar house that has become an international chain — go for the pudding counter, not the legend.
street-food|Hafız Mustafa 1864.body: The house's own About page tells a story of custody rather than bloodline: the ahi guild tradition of Hacı İsmail Hakkı Bey, then Cemil Bey, "son of Hafız Mustafa," trading as Çikolat Cemil, then Hacı Avni Ongurlar taking it on. The same page makes an unusual claim for a sweet shop — that it was the first to make poğaça, the salted breakfast pastry — and counts "159 years," which puts the writing at 2023. It is now a large operation: 19 branches listed, 15 of them in Istanbul (Bahçekapı-Eminönü, Sirkeci, Nuruosmaniye, Beyazıt, İstiklal, Taksim, Pera, Üsküdar, Galataport among them), plus five in Dubai and one in London. Two Istanbul branches are recorded in OpenStreetMap as trading 24 hours. The tell — Skip the window display and order from the pudding side: kazandibi, sütlaç, and the kadayıf. The Hamidiye Caddesi shop at No. 84 in Sirkeci opens at six in the morning, which makes it the most useful address in this section for anyone off an early boat. Expect tourist pricing and a queue at every central branch; the sweets are honest, the theatre is not. Hamidiye Cad. No:84, Hobyar Mah., Sirkeci, 34112 Fatih (14 other Istanbul branches) · Mon–Sun 06:00–22:30 at Hamidiye Cad. (OpenStreetMap); İstiklal Cad. 121 and Hüdavendigar Cad. recorded as 24/7

street-food|Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası.name: Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası
street-food|Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası.teaser: Künefe cooked the Antakya way, one street off İstiklal, at a house that came north from Hatay.
street-food|Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası.body: Two Istanbul rooms, both verified from the restaurant's own site: İstiklal Caddesi No:39 in Beyoğlu, opposite the French Consulate, and Nispetiye Caddesi No:18 out in Etiler. Künefe is the Hatay dessert and the reason to end a meal here rather than walk on — shredded kadayıf packed around fresh, unsalted, unaged cheese, baked in a shallow copper dish until both faces are dark, then drowned in syrup at the pass. The only credential the house advertises is a TripAdvisor certificate from 2015, which proves nothing at all; judge it on what arrives. OpenStreetMap places the POI just behind the avenue on Meşelik Sokağı, so aim for the İstiklal frontage and expect to turn the corner. The tell — Order the künefe at the end and eat it the moment it lands — it is only itself while the cheese still pulls, and it dies within minutes of the copper. One dish between two after a full Hatay table is enough. Do not order it to take away. İstiklal Cad. No:39 (opposite the French Consulate), Katip Mustafa Çelebi Mah., 34433 Beyoğlu; second room at Nispetiye Cad. No:18 · Not published

street-food|Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir.name: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir
street-food|Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir.teaser: Istanbul's oldest sugar counter, and the one claim about it that the historians will not sign.
street-food|Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir.body: The company's account: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir came to Constantinople from Kastamonu and opened in Bahçekapı in 1777; three generations of the family served as Şekerci Başı, head confectioner to the Ottoman palace; five generations have kept the Bahçekapı shop, which grew from a single room to 88 square metres by swallowing the spice shop next door. Where to be careful is the invention story. The Oxford Companion to Food is blunt — "although Bekir is often credited with the invention, there is no real evidence for it" — and Persian recipes using starch and sugar predate him by centuries. What is not in dispute is that the house still trades: eight points across Istanbul and Ankara, with the İstiklal Caddesi shop recorded open 08:00–21:00 daily and a Kadıköy counter on Muvakkıthane Caddesi. The tell — Ask for lokum cut from the tray rather than a sealed box: sakızlı (mastic) and gül (rose) plain, fıstıklı if you want the pistachio. The second counter is the one people walk past — akide şekeri, the hard palace candy the shop was making before lokum, plus helva and badem ezmesi. The historic address is Bahçekapı, off Hamidiye Caddesi; everything else is a branch. Hamidiye Cad., Hobyar Mah., Bahçekapı-Sirkeci, 34112 Fatih; branches at İstiklal Cad. 83, Beyoğlu and Muvakkıthane Cad. 14-16, Kadıköy · İstiklal Cad. branch Mon–Sun 08:00–21:00 (OpenStreetMap); the house publishes no hours

street-food|Şekerci Cafer Erol.name: Şekerci Cafer Erol
street-food|Şekerci Cafer Erol.teaser: 1807 on the sign, and a Kadıköy counter that still sells hard candy out of jars by weight.
street-food|Şekerci Cafer Erol.body: The house trades on "1807'den beri" and describes itself as keeping "İstanbul'un en köklü şekerleme geleneği" — the city's deepest-rooted confectionery tradition. Its catalogue reads less like a dessert menu than an inventory of Ottoman sugar work: lokumlar, akide şekerleri, ezmeler, helva, drajeler, nugat, bal ve reçel. The Kadıköy shop is the anchor and OpenStreetMap places it at Yasa Caddesi 19 in Osmanağa Mahallesi, a two-minute walk from the ferry pier. The house has since opened in Galataport, Ortaköy, İstinye Park, Emaar Square and London, which is exactly why the small Kadıköy counter is the one to walk to. The tell — Akide şekeri weighed out of the jars — the boiled palace candy, in the flavours the shop happens to have running — and badem ezmesi. Buy a mixed hundred grams rather than a boxed assortment; the box is for gifts, the paper bag is for the ferry back. Yasa Cad. No:19, Osmanağa Mah., 34714 Kadıköy (second Kadıköy shop at Tütüncü Mehmet Efendi Cad. 91, Göztepe) · Not published as shop hours; the site lists a weekday order window 09:30–17:00

street-food|Saray Muhallebicisi.name: Saray Muhallebicisi
street-food|Saray Muhallebicisi.teaser: A milk-pudding house, not a patisserie — opened in Kasımpaşa in 1935 to feed Beyoğlu properly.
street-food|Saray Muhallebicisi.body: Founded in 1935 by Hüseyin Topbaş with a stated aim that has survived on the company's own page in the original wording: "Beyoğlu'nda zarif hanımefendi ve beyefendilere tatlıların en güzelini yedirmek" — to feed the elegant ladies and gentlemen of Beyoğlu the finest of desserts. It took fourteen years to make the move that mattered, relocating onto Beyoğlu proper in 1949. The house now counts 21 branches, around 1,400 staff and more than a hundred flavours, and names bal kaymağı, fresh bread, tea and börek among the things it is known for. The İstiklal Caddesi room is the one with the history; the rest are the chain that history paid for. The tell — Order what a muhallebici exists for and what a patisserie cannot make: tavuk göğsü, the pudding thickened with shredded chicken breast until you cannot find it, and kazandibi, the same pudding scorched on the bottom of the pan and served caramelised side up. If it is morning, bal kaymak with bread instead — the house puts it first on its own list. İstiklal Cad., Asmalı Mescit Mah., 34430 Beyoğlu (21 branches in total) · Not published

street-food|Baylan Pastanesi.name: Baylan Pastanesi
street-food|Baylan Pastanesi.teaser: The republic's oldest pâtisserie, and one dessert that was invented inside it in 1954.
street-food|Baylan Pastanesi.body: Opened in 1923 by Filip Lenas, a Greek of Albanian origin, with his cousin Yorgi Kiriçi — first in Deva Çıkmazı under the name Loryan, the Turkish ear's rendering of "Le Orient" — and moved onto İstiklal Caddesi, into the Luvr Apartmanı, in 1928. The Kadıköy branch that most people now mean by "Baylan" was opened in 1961 by Mikail Lenas. The Kup Griye is the house's own: created by Harry Lenas in 1954, vanilla and caramel ice cream under whipped cream, honeyed almonds and caramel sauce, served with a kedidili biscuit. The business passed to the Altınmarka group, owner of Kahve Dünyası, in 2009 and has kept opening rooms since — Galataport in 2021, Kız Kulesi in 2024 — and its site was live and carrying a 2026 copyright line when checked. The tell — Kup Griye, sitting down, at the Kadıköy shop on Muvakkıthane Caddesi. Ask for it by name; it is the only thing here you cannot get somewhere else, and it is the reason to take a table rather than a paper bag. Note the address carefully — the Hacı Bekir counter is four doors along the same street. Muvakkıthane Cad. No:19, Caferağa Mah., 34710 Kadıköy — tel +90 216 346 63 50 · Not published

street-food|Vefa Bozacısı.name: Vefa Bozacısı
street-food|Vefa Bozacısı.teaser: Thick, pale, faintly sour fermented millet, poured at the address that turned it into a trade in September 1876.
street-food|Vefa Bozacısı.body: The house's own tarihçe: Hacı Sadık Bey arrived in Istanbul from Prizren in 1870 and spent six winters carrying boza through the streets in copper vessels before opening, in September 1876, what it calls the first registered boza shop in the world. He fixed the style the city still expects and describes it precisely — thick-bodied, pale yellow, caught at the moment the fermentation bubbles first rise, with a very light sourness. His son İsmail Hakkı came into the production; the house says the fourth generation runs it now, and it is the only boza shop of its era still trading. The same firm makes vinegars, üzüm şırası and şerbet, which is what carries it through the months when nobody wants boza. The tell — One glass of boza, standing, taken the customary way — dusted with cinnamon, with roasted leblebi to chew alongside. This is cold-weather drinking: come between October and April and the shop is doing what it exists for; come in August and you are buying vinegar. A glass said to have been used by Atatürk is kept on display. Vefa Cad. No:66, 34134 Fatih — tel +90 212 519 49 22 · OpenStreetMap records Mon–Sun 08:00–22:00; the house publishes no hours of its own

street-food|Mado.name: Mado
street-food|Mado.teaser: The Kahramanmaraş ice cream you cut with a knife — and the chain that industrialised it, which is both the point and the limit.
street-food|Mado.body: The company's own history page traces the thing back to snow carried down from Ahır Dağı above Kahramanmaraş, which "Osman Ağa" enriched with milk, honey and salep. His descendants Mehmet, Atilla and Erdal Kanbur turned it into an industry — Yaşar Kanbur began by making and selling ice cream from a small shop next to the Aras bus garage — with a Kahramanmaraş factory in 1965, machines in 1970, the MARDO brand in 1984 and real modernisation in 1989. The house dates itself to 1850. Two ingredients do all the work: goat milk, which is why the company runs its own "MADO Beyazı" goat farm, and salep, the ground orchid tuber that makes the ice cream stretch and refuse to melt. Demand for salep has thinned the region's wild orchids badly enough that Turkey banned its export. The tell — Ask for kesme dondurma — the cut ice cream, served in slabs with a knife and fork rather than scooped — and take it sade, plain, so the goat milk and the salep are the flavour. The cone is the tourist version. No single flagship is worth crossing the city for: this is a several-hundred-branch chain and any decent branch will show you what the texture is, which is precisely why it belongs here as a reference point rather than a destination. Branches across the city; no flagship verified

street-food|Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta.name: Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta
street-food|Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta.teaser: Moda's ice-cream counter, the one every Kadıköy list names — and the one entry here I could not confirm is trading.
street-food|Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta.body: What is actually on record: OpenStreetMap carries a point of interest named "Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta" on Moda Caddesi in Caferağa Mahallesi, Kadıköy, with the telephone +90 216 414 1880 attached. There is no company website, no published hours, and no dated confirmation from any source I trust that the counter was serving in August 2026. That is not a claim it has closed — closure would be a finding, and I do not have one. It is a gap, and the gap is the honest thing to publish rather than a confident pin. Every other entry in this section was checked against a live company website or a fetched history page on the date below; this one was not. The tell — Call +90 216 414 1880 before you take the ferry. If someone answers and the counter is running, it sits on Moda Caddesi as you walk down toward the sea. Treat this as a lead to check, not a booking — and if it does not answer, Baylan and Şekerci Cafer Erol are both a short walk back toward the pier and both were confirmed. Moda Cad., Caferağa Mah., 34710 Kadıköy (OpenStreetMap) Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

listening|The Listening Room at Arkestra.name: The Listening Room at Arkestra
listening|The Listening Room at Arkestra.teaser: A hi-fi room with a wall of vinyl on the upper floor of a one-star restaurant, in a 1960s villa in Etiler.
listening|The Listening Room at Arkestra.body: Arkestra occupies a former residential villa built in the 1960s and splits it three ways: the ground-floor restaurant with an open kitchen and courtyard, a 32-cover bistro called Ritmo with its own private entrance and mirrored ceilings, and the Listening Room upstairs. The Listening Room runs a weekly rotation where selectors either pull from the house record collection or bring their own, over craft cocktails, palm-tree feature walls and low tables. The honest catch, stated by the house: it currently welcomes restaurant guests only, so it is not a room you can walk into off the street. Cenk Debensason's kitchen took its MICHELIN star in 2024, which is what fills the building and, indirectly, what keeps the upstairs going. The tell — Eat downstairs first, then go up — that is the only way in. Ask which selector is on that night before you book; the programme is weekly, not resident. Dilhayat Sok. No:28, Etiler, Beşiktaş, İstanbul · Tue–Sat 18:00–01:00

listening|Kontra Plak.name: Kontra Plak
listening|Kontra Plak.teaser: An independent record shop trading on Yeni Çarşı since 2012, with a listening-room programme attached.
listening|Kontra Plak.body: Two doors from Galatasaray Lisesi on the street that has quietly become Beyoğlu's record row, Kontra carries new and second-hand Turkish and foreign vinyl, CDs, cassettes and music books in both Turkish and English, plus turntables, cartridges and headshells. Its own site was showing arrivals dated August 2026 when this guide checked, which is the only proof of life that matters for a shop. It runs named strands rather than one-off events — Dinleme Odası, the listening room; Kontra'da; Örümcek; Just Kids — and takes part in Record Store Day with in-store concerts. Context for why this matters: Lale Plak, open on Galip Dede Caddesi since 1954 and the shop where local musicians met, announced its closure by tweet and shut on 31 December 2019. Its owner Hakan Atala told Hürriyet the following January, "Burası müzisyenlerin buluşma yeriydi, içim buruk." The tell — Ask for the Turkish second-hand racks, not the reissue wall — the 1970s Anadolu pressings are the reason to be in this room rather than online. Time a visit to a Dinleme Odası night if the calendar allows. Tomtom Mah., Yeni Çarşı Cad. No:60/A, Galatasaray, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Daily 11:00–20:00

listening|Analog Kültür.name: Analog Kültür
listening|Analog Kültür.teaser: A record shop and studio on a Şahkulu cul-de-sac that also cuts one-off lathe records.
listening|Analog Kültür.body: It opened on Record Store Day 2014, when DJ and producer Kaan Düzarat went looking for somewhere to move his studio and decided the studio should be a record shop too. His reasoning, in his own words: in late 2013 there were very few shops in the city and none where you could reliably find good electronic music, old or new, so he built a room to share whatever passed his own filter. About eighty percent of the archive is second-hand — 45s and albums from the seventies and eighties, house, techno, drum and bass, synthwave and krautrock from the nineties and 2000s, then jazz, funk, soul, bossa, Middle and Far Eastern records, rock and classical. The shop also carries a proper hi-fi department (amplifiers, turntables, cartridges, reel-to-reel, speakers) and, with Eazycut Records, cuts lathe records to order. Coffee is part of the deal. The tell — Bring a recording you want on vinyl and ask about the lathe cut — call between 12:00 and 20:00. Otherwise dig the Turkish section; Düzarat has been actively buying domestic pressings as local production revived. Şahkulu, Seraskerci Çk. No:4 D:A, 34421 Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Lathe-cut enquiries 12:00–20:00; shop hours not published

listening|Akmar Pasajı.name: Akmar Pasajı
listening|Akmar Pasajı.teaser: The Kadıköy arcade that has been the city's second-hand book and record warren since 1982.
listening|Akmar Pasajı.body: It stands on the site of the Özel Marmara Koleji, a school founded in 1957 whose building was damaged by adjacent construction in 1980, demolished, and replaced in 1982 by an office block with shops on the lower floors. The name is a splice: Akdik, the owning family's surname, and syllables lifted from the school's. It runs through between Mühürdar Caddesi and Neşet Ömer Sokak, which is why half of Kadıköy uses it as a shortcut without ever stopping, and it holds a specific place in Istanbul's fanzine, metal and rock history — enough that in 1999 it was subject to a police raid on unfounded claims, with those arrested later found to have no connection to the matter. Second-hand booksellers dominate; music shops sit among them. The tell — Go for the sahaf stalls and the two music shops rather than a specific address — individual tenants turn over, the arcade does not. Walk in from Mühürdar and out onto Neşet Ömer. Caferağa Mah., Mühürdar Cad., Akmar Pasajı, Kadıköy, İstanbul · Shop hours vary by tenant

listening|Kadıköy Plak Kulübü.name: Kadıköy Plak Kulübü
listening|Kadıköy Plak Kulübü.teaser: A working Asian-side record shop, open every day, that also sells the turntable.
listening|Kadıköy Plak Kulübü.body: It sits in the Kadıköy İş Merkezi on Neşet Ömer Sokak — the far end of the same short block that Akmar Pasajı empties into, so the two are one walk. The shop splits its stock plainly: Turkish records, foreign records, rock, plus CDs, cassettes and turntables, and it buys second-hand collections in as well as selling them, which is what keeps the Turkish racks moving. Its own storefront was showing live pricing and current stock at this check. Between this and the arcade you can do the entire Kadıköy record run in under an hour without crossing a main road. The tell — Sell as well as buy — bringing a collection in is how you get shown the back stock. If you need a deck rather than records, this is the shop on the Asian side that carries them. Caferağa Mah., Neşet Ömer Sok. No:1, Kadıköy İş Merkezi, Dükkan No:27, Kadıköy, İstanbul · Open daily, per the shop's own listing

listening|Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi.name: Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi
listening|Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi.teaser: A Balık Pazarı meyhane with live Turkish music every night and a table that has been reserved since 1938.
listening|Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi.body: The house was founded before the Republic was declared and, by its own account, was named by Atatürk himself — take that as the family's claim, not a documented fact, but the table it says he sat at is still kept permanently reserved, and the house has traded under the name since 1923. It is one street off the Beyoğlu fish market on Sahne Sokak, open every day from noon to midnight, with Turkish traditional live music listed as a standing feature rather than a weekend booking. The meze card carries the old Istanbul minority repertoire that most of Beyoğlu has quietly dropped: topik with caramelised onion and cinnamon, çiroz cut with dill and vinegar, kabak çiçeği dolması from Aegean flowers. The tell — Start with topik and çiroz — the Armenian and Greek plates are the reason to be in this room rather than a newer meyhane. Go late enough that the musicians are working the tables; the rakı is poured with water, not over it. Kamer Hatun Cad., Sahne Sok. No:27, Balık Pazarı, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Daily 12:00–00:00

listening|Babylon.name: Babylon
listening|Babylon.teaser: The city's long-running live room in the old Bomonti brewery quarter, booking hard through winter 2026.
listening|Babylon.body: Time Out Istanbul calls it the city's premier live music venue, and the programme backs it rather than the reputation carrying it: at this check the calendar ran from the Babylon Soundgarden Festival at Bonus Parkorman on 22 and 23 August through Ben LaMar Gay Ensemble on 1 October, Yazmin Lacey on 7 October, Kassa Overall on 9 October, the Samora Pinderhughes Quintet with Elena Pinderhughes on 10 October, Kelly Lee Owens DJ set on 16 October, and Bilal marking twenty-five years of 1st Born Second on 11 December. That is a jazz and left-field booking policy, not a covers room. It sits on Silahşör Caddesi in Bomonti, which it did as much as anything to turn into a nightlife district when it moved out of Beyoğlu. The tell — Buy the ticket before you travel — these are single-night international bookings, not a residency. Check whether the date is at Babylon itself or out at Bonus Parkorman; the festival dates are not in the venue. Silahşör Cad., Cumhuriyet Mah., Bomonti, Şişli, İstanbul · By event

listening|Fiba Salon İKSV.name: Fiba Salon İKSV
listening|Fiba Salon İKSV.teaser: The İKSV concert hall that has just changed its name for the first time since 2010.
listening|Fiba Salon İKSV.body: Open since 2010 as Salon İKSV in the foundation's Nejat Eczacıbaşı building on Sadi Konuralp Caddesi, it takes the name Fiba Salon İKSV from the autumn 2026 season under a sponsorship with Fiba Grubu. İKSV's own announcement is unusually candid about what the room is for: its chair describes it as where a great many young people first encountered the foundation. The partnership widens the programme beyond concerts into theatre, literature talks, science evenings and jazz-club nights, so the booking pattern you find will not match what the room did five years ago. It is a proper seated hall run by the organisation behind the Istanbul film, music, jazz, theatre and biennial festivals, not a bar. The tell — Check the programme under the new name — searching the old one still resolves, but the listings that matter are on fibasaloniksv.com. The new jazz-club evenings are the strand to watch. Nejat Eczacıbaşı Binası, Sadi Konuralp Cad., Şişhane, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · By event

listening|KOLI Art Space.name: KOLI Art Space
listening|KOLI Art Space.teaser: An artist-run space with a programme that runs late.
listening|KOLI Art Space.body: Founded 2021 by Elçin Acun and Yasemin Kalaycı. Non-profit production and exhibition space supporting feminist and queer artists, on identity and gender fluidity. Showed at Contemporary Istanbul CI BLOOM 2026. Kadıköy Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-11 — call ahead.

listening|NOKS (formerly TOZ).body: Began 2015 as TOZ, founded by Ece Elder, Elvan Ekren, Sinem Dişli and Volkan Kızıltunç; NOKS after 2018, run by Kızıltunç and Ekren. listening|Nublu Istanbul / Nublu Records.name: Nublu Istanbul / Nublu Records

listening|Nublu Istanbul / Nublu Records.body: İlhan Erşahin's label and room, founded 2005 as the extension of the Nublu sound from New York's Lower East Side. listening|Nardis Jazz Club.name: Nardis Jazz Club
listening|Nardis Jazz Club.teaser: The city's longest-running dedicated jazz club, below Galata Tower.
listening|Nardis Jazz Club.body: Roughly 120 seats at the foot of the Galata Tower, live jazz from local and international acts practically every night. Programming already listed into 2026–27. THE jazz room in Istanbul, and the reason Wednesday is on the week grid Kuledibi Sok., Galata, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Weekdays 21:30–00:30 · weekends 22:30–01:30

listening|Solera Winery.name: Solera Winery
listening|Solera Winery.teaser: An all-Turkish list in a narrow Beyoğlu room, 300 metres off İstiklal.
listening|Solera Winery.body: Opened 1 October 2011 on Yeni Çarşı Caddesi and pours only domestic producers — red, white, rosé, sparkling and fruit wine, no imports on the card. Since 2013 the house has farmed its own vineyard at Gaziköy in Tekirdağ, on the Marmara shore of Thrace, and runs its own Şarap Tadımı tasting evenings walking guests through Turkish varieties region by region. This is the room where the argument that Turkey has a wine culture rather than a wine industry gets made in glasses rather than in print. The Thracian producers you will meet here — Chamlija, founded 2007 by Mustafa Çamlıca on the decomposed granite of the Strandja massif in Kırklareli, labels drawn by his daughter İrem — are farming indigenous Papazkarası alongside the international grapes the domestic market once demanded. The tell — Ask for the by-the-glass flight of native grapes rather than a bottle: Öküzgözü and Boğazkere from the east, Narince from Tokat, Papazkarası from Thrace. Kitchen runs to cheese and charcuterie boards, salads, pasta and köfte if you want to stay. Tomtom Mah., Yeni Çarşı Cad. No:44, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Daily 13:00–01:00

listening|Sensus Wine Boutique.name: Sensus Wine Boutique
listening|Sensus Wine Boutique.teaser: A stone cellar at the foot of the Galata Tower that sells the cheese as seriously as the wine.
listening|Sensus Wine Boutique.body: The Galata room on Büyük Hendek Caddesi was the first; the business now runs thirteen shops across Türkiye, from Kavaklıdere in Ankara to Çeşme, Bursa and İzmir, and says so on its own site. The buying is done on quarterly tasting tours through seven Turkish wine regions, direct from boutique producers, and the same trips bring back the cheese, charcuterie, honey, olives and oil that fill the counter. It is a shop that lets you sit down, not a bar with a shelf — which is why the pairing plate is the point rather than an afterthought. Time Out Istanbul has carried it for years as the Turkish wine-and-cheese address by the tower. The tell — Order a tasting flight against a regional cheese plate — the counter cuts from producers the buyers have actually visited. Take a bottle away afterwards; the retail price is the reason to buy here rather than drink here. Bereketzade Mah., Kuledibi, Büyük Hendek Cad. No:5, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Not published on the house site — call ahead

listening|Viktor Levi Şarap Evi.name: Viktor Levi Şarap Evi
listening|Viktor Levi Şarap Evi.teaser: A garden wine house in Moda with a founder's story and a fourteen-year gap in the middle of it.
listening|Viktor Levi Şarap Evi.body: Viktor Levi was the son of a Gelibolu sardine family who moved into grapes on Bozcaada, then opened his own şaraphane in Istanbul after the established houses — Pano, Diamandi, İzmirli, Sofaki — refused him a fair price for his wine. He ran it until his death in 1967; his cousin Yasef held it until 1985, then left for America and the doors shut. It stayed closed for fourteen years until Fevzi Büyükerol bought the property in 1999 and spent about a year rebuilding the interior to the original materials and style before reopening it in Moda. The garden behind Damacı Sokak is the reason people stay for four hours; the house wines are the reason they came. The tell — The house-labelled wines, drunk in the garden rather than the salon. The kitchen is a full restaurant — order to the wine, not the other way round. Caferağa Mah., Moda Cad., Damacı Sok. No:4, Kadıköy, İstanbul · Not published on the house site — call ahead

listening|Orient Bar, Pera Palace.name: Orient Bar, Pera Palace
listening|Orient Bar, Pera Palace.teaser: The lobby-floor bar of the hotel built in 1892 for passengers off the Orient Express — currently dark for the season.
listening|Orient Bar, Pera Palace.body: As of this check the hotel's own page states the Orient Bar is out of service until the end of the summer season, so do not walk up expecting it. What is open in its place is the Orient Terrace on the ground floor, lobby side, over the Golden Horn: 09:00 to 23:00 for the full menu and 23:00 to 02:00 for drinks only. Upstairs, Room 411 is kept as the Agatha Christie room — 46 square metres of period furniture, a library of her books in several languages and a replica of her typewriter, and it is bookable as a guest room rather than roped off as a museum. Smart casual on the terrace; the hotel enforces it. The tell — Since the bar itself is shut, take the terrace at dusk for the Golden Horn light and the fresh-fruit cocktails, and ask at reception whether 411 is free to look at. Meşrutiyet Cad. No:52, Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Orient Bar: closed until end of summer season. Orient Terrace: daily 09:00–23:00, drinks to 02:00 Heads up — A limited run — check the end date before you plan around it.

listening|Kubbeli Lounge, Pera Palace.name: Kubbeli Lounge, Pera Palace
listening|Kubbeli Lounge, Pera Palace.teaser: Afternoon tea under the domes, with a pianist named on the hotel's own page.
listening|Kubbeli Lounge, Pera Palace.body: The Kubbeli — kubbe is Turkish for dome — is the high-ceilinged salon the hotel built its social life around, and it is the room to use while the Orient Bar is shut. The house lists traditional afternoon tea accompanied by the piano of Aslı Güral, which is unusual: hotels rarely name the musician.
