The money — No price published. Kadıköy fal cafes generally work on a table minimum plus a per-reading fee. Agree the figure before the cup is turned, and refuse an open-ended one. The catch — Three catches, and the first is that I could not confirm this business is still trading. Its website resolves but its security certificate has expired and the footer still reads 2013; the address, phone and hours below come from that unmaintained page and nothing else. Ring before you cross the water. Second, expect Turkish — none of the Kadıköy fal cafes advertise an English-speaking reader, and a reading through a translator is not a reading. Third, and seriously: this cafe advertises medyums alongside its falcıs, and the medyum trade in Turkey sits next door to a real fraud industry that works on people in trouble. A cup read over a coffee is harmless entertainment. Anything that escalates into paid follow-up sessions, lifting a curse, or a bank transfer is a fraud, and the correct response is to stand up and leave. Caferağa Mah., Serasker Cad., Pavlonya Sk. No:23/3, 34710 Kadıköy · +90 533 777 72 32 (per the cafe's own site, which appears not to have been maintained for years) · Listed as seven days, 11:30–21:00, on the cafe's own site — a page last dated 2013 and serving an expired certificate. Treat as indicative only and telephone first. Heads up — Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

rituals|Türk kahvesi — Fazıl Bey, and th.name: Türk kahvesi — Fazıl Bey, and the cup turned over
rituals|Türk kahvesi — Fazıl Bey, and th.teaser: One small cup, twenty minutes, and a foam you can judge the whole thing on.
rituals|Türk kahvesi — Fazıl Bey, and th.body: Turkish coffee is judged on the köpük, the fine head of foam, and the foam is a function of heat control: the cezve is brought up slowly and lifted off as it rises, two or three times, and never allowed to boil over. Get that wrong and you are drinking boiled coffee. Fazıl Bey's is the everyday Kadıköy counter that does it properly at an everyday price — a market-side room rather than a set piece, open eight in the morning until midnight, seven days, which makes it one of the few places in this section a chef finishing a shift can actually reach. Sand-brewing — kumda kahve, the cezve set into a tray of hot sand so nothing scorches on the base — is the version you will see photographed; be aware it has become largely a visitor-facing presentation in this city, and this guide could not verify any particular old bazaar house as still doing it. How it works — Order by sugar, which goes in before the boil and can never be added after: sade for none, az şekerli for a little, orta for medium, çok şekerli for sweet. Water arrives alongside and is drunk first, to clear the mouth. Do not stir. Drink to the last centimetre and stop — the rest is grounds. Then, if you want, invert the cup onto the saucer and let it cool. The tell — Judge the cup on the foam, not the strength. A proper one arrives with an even, fine head across the whole surface; a boiled one arrives flat, with a ring of scum at the edge. Etiquette — It is one small cup and it is meant to take twenty minutes. Do not order a second immediately. Turkish coffee closes a meal here, it does not open one. The money — Not published by either house. Fazıl Bey is an ordinary neighbourhood counter and is the benchmark for what a cup should cost; anything inside the Grand Bazaar will be a multiple of it. Ask before you order. The catch — On the Grand Bazaar alternative: Şark Kahvesi is a genuine old bazaar coffeehouse and is mapped inside the bazaar on Zenneciler Sokağı, not on the main artery as is often written. This guide could not verify its founding date, its brewing method or its current prices on 16 August 2026, and the recurring complaint about it in both Turkish and English is bazaar pricing — go for the vaulted room if you want the room, and do not expect value. Note also that the Grand Bazaar is shut on Sundays and public holidays, which catches people out, and that its hours are roughly 09:00–19:00 Monday to Saturday — confirm on the day. Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi, Serasker Cad., Caferağa, Kadıköy · tel 0216 346 16 15 · Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi: 08:00–24:00, seven days (the company's own site, read 16 Aug 2026; OpenStreetMap agrees, Mo–Su 08:00–24:00). Grand Bazaar: roughly 09:00–19:00 Monday–Saturday, closed Sundays and public holidays.

rituals|Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday.name: Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday
rituals|Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday.teaser: Twenty plates, three hours, and nothing else planned for the day. It is an appointment, not a breakfast.
rituals|Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday.body: This guide already explains what serpme kahvaltı is and where the word came from. What it does not tell you is that it functions as a scheduled event rather than a meal you drop into. The Istanbul version runs on Sunday from roughly ten in the morning to two in the afternoon; tables are held, not turned; and a serious kahvaltı house will not seat two people at a table for four at half past eleven without a booking. The structure matters practically: you make one decision, per person, and then the plates arrive together and keep arriving. There is no second round of ordering, no courses and no order of service. The commonest visitor mistake is treating it as a menu. How it works — Book, or be at the door when it opens. Order 'serpme kahvaltı, iki kişilik' — the count is people, not portions. The only thing you actually choose is the egg: menemen soft-scrambled with tomato and green pepper, sahanda yumurta fried in the pan, sucuklu yumurta with the cured sausage, or a plain omlet. Tea is poured and refilled without being asked and is normally included, but ask rather than assume. Turkish coffee comes at the end, which is the joke buried in the word kahvaltı — kahve altı, 'under coffee', the thing eaten before the cup. Two to three hours. Plan nothing after it. The tell — The markers of a serious table are bal kaymak — clotted buffalo cream under comb honey — eggs cooked to order rather than held in a chafing dish, and çay refilled before you notice the glass is empty. Add a bread basket replaced hot, and at least one plate you cannot identify. Etiquette — Do not ask for plates to be cleared as you go; the sprawl is the format. Do not ask for coffee at the start. Do not order à la carte alongside a serpme spread — it costs more and reads as a rejection of the thing you just sat down to. The money — Priced and displayed per person. No figure is given here — the spread between a neighbourhood house and a waterfront one, and between a weekday and a Sunday, is too wide for any single number to be honest. Read the board. The catch — The catch is arithmetic. Serpme is priced per head and quoted per head, so a table for two on a Sunday can cost more than dinner for two — read the board carefully, because the number on it is what one of you pays. The same house serving a weekday breakfast will put most of the same plates down for a fraction of it. The Bosphorus-front kahvaltı strips at Bebek, Çengelköy and Beşiktaş are where the price has run furthest ahead of the food and where the queue is longest. And for anyone working a boat with one day off: this eats the whole morning and most of the afternoon. It is the most time-expensive thing in this section by a distance, and it is worth doing exactly once. Beşiktaş, Bebek, Çengelköy, Moda — and every quarter's own version · Sunday roughly 10:00–14:00 is the institution. Kahvaltı houses generally serve from about 08:00 or 09:00; the better ones run breakfast into mid-afternoon, which is how to avoid the eleven o'clock crush — go at nine or go at three.

rituals|Rakı-balık — choosing the fish o.name: Rakı-balık — choosing the fish off the ice
rituals|Rakı-balık — choosing the fish o.teaser: The fish is not on the menu. It is on ice by the door, priced by the kilo you have not yet asked about.
rituals|Rakı-balık — choosing the fish o.body: The rakı table's spine is cold mezes, then hot mezes, then one fish — and the fish is chosen rather than ordered. In a balıkçı or a meyhane with a counter you walk to the ice at the entrance, point at what you want, and it is weighed in front of you before it goes on the grill. That single step is where visitors lose money in this city more reliably than anywhere else, because the fish is priced by the kilo, the per-kilo price is frequently not posted, and a lüfer that looked like one person's dinner arrives at nine hundred grams. Ask 'kilosu kaç?' before you point, and ask to see the scale. A house that will not show you the kilo price has already told you what kind of house it is. How it works — Rakı and cold water arrive together; the spirit is drunk diluted and turns milky as the water goes in, and the water glass stays beside it and is drunk alongside. If ice is used it goes in last, on top of the mix — never pour rakı straight onto a glass of ice. Then cold mezes, unhurried, for the best part of an hour. Then hot mezes. Then the fish, grilled whole with nothing on it. Season decides everything: palamut from September, lüfer peaking in October, hamsi through December. Anything glossy and cheap in July is farmed or flown. At a market counter rather than a restaurant, ask 'temizler misiniz?' to have it cleaned. The tell — The tell of a real table is the pace: four hours, nobody's plate cleared early, and the drinking set by the food. Ordering rakı and then eating fast is the visitor's giveaway more than anything you say. Etiquette — You never drink rakı without food. The water glass stays full and is drunk alongside, not after. When glasses touch, the rim of yours goes lower than the elder's — a small gesture, and it is noticed. The money — Priced by the kilo and it moves weekly with the catch and the season. There is no fair number to quote and anyone quoting one is guessing. Ask the kilo price and watch the scale — that is the entire defence. The catch — The per-kilo trick is real, common and entirely legal. Kumkapı has the worst reputation for it. The Beyoğlu Balık Pazarı row off Sahne Sokak has thinned into meyhane tables and stalls, so it is now more restaurant than market. The counters that still work as markets — Kadıköy off Güneşlibahçe Sokak, Beşiktaş Çarşı, Üsküdar Balıkçılar Çarşısı — are where the price is honest, and are also where nobody will pour you a rakı. On buying your own fish and having it cooked nearby: some grills next to the fishmongers will do it and some will not, it is not a standard citywide service, and it is worth asking rather than assuming in either direction — do not plan an evening around it. Kadıköy's fish row off Güneşlibahçe Sokak · Beşiktaş Çarşı · Üsküdar Balıkçılar Çarşısı · Fish counters are a morning business and most are finished by early afternoon. The rakı table is an evening one and starts late — Thursday is the night, per this guide's own week.

landmarks|Sultanahmet Meydanı — the Hipp.name: Sultanahmet Meydanı — the Hippodrome
landmarks|Sultanahmet Meydanı — the Hipp.teaser: You are standing on the racetrack — about 450 metres of it, under two metres of fill.
landmarks|Sultanahmet Meydanı — the Hipp.body: Septimius Severus laid a hippodrome here around AD 203; Constantine rebuilt it in 324–330 as the centrepiece of his new capital — roughly 450 by 130 metres, stands for some 100,000 people. The long oval of today's square is the track itself, and the three monuments standing in their sunken pits mark the spina, the central barrier the chariots turned around: Thutmose III's granite obelisk (the guide's Curiosities section tells its story), the Serpent Column brought from Delphi where it celebrated the Greek victory over Persia at Plataea — the oldest Greek object in the city — and the Walled Obelisk, stripped of its gilded bronze by the Fourth Crusade in 1204. The pits exist because the modern ground sits about two metres above the ancient track. The Nika riots began here in 532 and burned half the city; the last recorded race ran in 1200. What the square is for: reading fifteen centuries in a single flat ten-minute walk, free, at any hour — the German Fountain of 1900, Kaiser Wilhelm II's gift, closes the north end. The tell — The Serpent Column, from Delphi — cast from the weapons of the Persians defeated at Plataea in 479 BC The catch — From mid-morning to dusk this is the hardest-worked square in Turkey: carpet touts, sudden new friends steering you toward a shop, dropped shoe-shine brushes. Come at 07:00 before the coaches, or after dark when it is floodlit and the trade has gone home. Walk like you have an appointment. Sultanahmet, Fatih · Open ground — walkable at any hour, free

landmarks|Beyazıt Meydanı.name: Beyazıt Meydanı
landmarks|Beyazıt Meydanı.teaser: The university's square, laid over the biggest forum of Roman Constantinople.
landmarks|Beyazıt Meydanı.body: Under the paving lies the Forum of Theodosius — the Forum Tauri — and around the square stands a full Ottoman-to-Republic ensemble: the Beyazıt II Mosque on one side, the Neo-Renaissance arch of Istanbul University's main gate by the French architect Bourgeois on the other, the Beyazıt Tower rising behind it, and the Beyazıt State Library of 1884 between them — whose renovation turned up the remains of a Byzantine church beneath the floor. The square itself was comprehensively rebuilt and reopened on 6 October 2022, and the redesign worked: it is now the calmest large open space in the old city — students on the steps, seed-sellers and their pigeon clouds, old men on benches under the plane trees on the mosque flank, where the lane dips down to the Sahaflar book market (which has its own card in this guide). What it is for: sitting still in the old city without buying anything. Best in late afternoon, when the light comes low across the mosque courtyard and the university empties. The tell — Tea under the plane trees between the mosque and the book market The catch — The Ordu Caddesi side is a tram-and-traffic hinge, and the square has a long history as the city's protest ground — on demonstration days expect police barriers and skip it. Beyazıt, Fatih · Open ground — walkable at any hour, free

landmarks|Ortaköy Meydanı.name: Ortaköy Meydanı
landmarks|Ortaköy Meydanı.teaser: The one square in the city that sits directly on the Bosphorus, with a Balyan mosque on the quay.
landmarks|Ortaköy Meydanı.body: The Büyük Mecidiye Camii — everyone says Ortaköy Mosque — was built 1854–56 for Sultan Abdülmecid I by Garabet and Nigoğayos Balyan, the Armenian father-and-son architects of Dolmabahçe, and it stands not near the water but on it, ornate European-Baroque stone carving straight out of the strait. A three-year restoration brought it back on 6 June 2014 and it works as a mosque; enter outside prayer times. Behind it, the small square and its lanes run the famous kumpir stalls — the loaded baked potato is Ortaköy's street dish — and café tables to the water's edge. What the square is for: the single frame the city puts on postcards, the 1850s mosque against the first Bosphorus bridge (15 Temmuz Şehitler Köprüsü), and ferries sliding between them. Best on a weekday morning, when you get the quay to yourself and the fishermen; sunset is the photograph but you will share it. The tell — The mosque and the bridge in one look, from the quay rail The catch — Weekend afternoons are shoulder-to-shoulder, and the front-row café tables price the view into the menu. Know the recent history too: in November 2025 a visiting family of four died after a day that ended with Ortaköy kumpir and midye — forensics ultimately traced the deaths to pesticide fumigation at their hotel, not the food, but inspectors sealed several stalls for hygiene in the sweep that followed and the quay stood empty for weeks. The row trades again; pick a busy stall with turnover, and stand at the water. Ortaköy, Beşiktaş · Open ground — walkable at any hour; mosque outside prayer times

landmarks|Gülhane Parkı.name: Gülhane Parkı
landmarks|Gülhane Parkı.teaser: The outer garden of Topkapı Palace, and the city's oldest public park.
landmarks|Gülhane Parkı.body: This was the wooded outer garden of Topkapı, opened to the public by the municipality in 1912 — the oldest public park in Istanbul, just under ten hectares falling from the palace walls toward Sarayburnu, where the Bosphorus meets the Marmara. Its name is in the history books: the Tanzimat edict, the decree that began the empire's modernisation, was read at Gülhane on 3 November 1839. The renovations of the 2000s stripped out the old zoo and funfair, and what is left is the right thing — lawns, very old planes with grey herons in them, and the Goths Column, a Roman victory monument, standing near the lower end. On the park's edges sit the Alay Köşkü on the outer wall and the Islamic science and technology museum in the former palace stables; the Archaeological Museums (which have their own card) are entered from here too. What it is for: the only place to feel the palace's ground without a ticket, and the shortest escape from Sultanahmet's crowds — two minutes from the tram. The tell — The walk downhill under the planes to the Goths Column and the sea The catch — A public city park with gates — go in daylight; we did not verify posted closing times. Know that the municipality shuts its parks outright on severe-storm alerts (Gülhane was closed for one in August 2025) — on an orange-warning day, don't bother. Gülhane, Fatih — below Topkapı

landmarks|Emirgan Korusu.name: Emirgan Korusu
landmarks|Emirgan Korusu.tag: Khedive's grove · tulips in April · free
landmarks|Emirgan Korusu.teaser: A khedive's exile estate above the Bosphorus — and in April, the densest flowerbed in Turkey.
landmarks|Emirgan Korusu.body: Forty-seven hectares of grove above the Emirgan shore, once the estate of Khedive İsmail Paşa of Egypt, who lived out his exile here; the city took it over in the 1940s and the İBB runs it now. His three 19th-century pavilions survive, restored 1979–83 — the Sarı Köşk (the yellow one, the park's centrepiece, run as a café by the municipal operator Beltur since 1997), the Beyaz Köşk and the Pembe Köşk, all trading as municipal cafés and function rooms. The tulip reality: since 2005 the April tulip festival has made Emirgan its main stage, millions of bulbs in set-piece beds — it is genuinely spectacular and genuinely mobbed, with the shore road jammed on festival weekends. Any other month you get one of the great groves of the city nearly to yourself: steep paths, ponds, huge pines, and the Bosphorus flashing between trunks. Pairs naturally with the Sakıp Sabancı Museum at the bottom of the hill (see the crafts pages). The tell — The Sarı Köşk seen across the pond, out of tulip season, in silence The catch — April means crowds and parking misery — come by bus or ferry-plus-walk. Pavilion café hours unverified; the grove itself is the point. Emirgan, Sarıyer

landmarks|Fethi Paşa Korusu.name: Fethi Paşa Korusu
landmarks|Fethi Paşa Korusu.tag: Asian-side grove · the bridge view · free
landmarks|Fethi Paşa Korusu.teaser: The Asian shore's vizier's grove, with the first bridge filling the whole view.
landmarks|Fethi Paşa Korusu.body: Some thirteen hectares of wooded hillside dropping to the Bosphorus just north of Üsküdar, named for Fethi Ahmed Paşa, the Ottoman vizier whose estate this was. After decades of neglect it was renewed and opened fully to the public, and it is now the local answer to the European shore's manicured parks — steeper, quieter, and pointed straight at the water: the terraces look across at Ortaköy and the European towers with the first Bosphorus bridge overhead, close enough to read the traffic. A municipal social facility — the Fethipaşa Sosyal Tesisi — trades inside the grove with tea and breakfast. What it is for: the postcard panorama without a single tour group. This is where Üsküdar families do Sunday breakfast; a visitor here has left the circuit entirely. Walk in from Kuzguncuk's one street (which has its own card) and the morning makes itself. The tell — Breakfast-hour view of the bridge from the upper terrace The catch — Paths are steep and shade is real — flat shoes. Facility hours unverified; the terraces and the view are free and always there. Paşalimanı, Üsküdar — between Kuzguncuk and Sultantepe

landmarks|Büyük Çamlıca.name: Büyük Çamlıca
landmarks|Büyük Çamlıca.teaser: The hill of the old Istanbul songs — read honestly, now shared with a tower and the country's biggest mosque.
landmarks|Büyük Çamlıca.body: At 288 metres, Büyük Çamlıca is the classic lookout of the Asian side, with the whole lower Bosphorus and the mouth of the Golden Horn laid out below. The honest read first: the romantic bare hilltop of the songs is gone. The summit ridge now carries the 369-metre Çamlıca Tower (opened 2021, a broadcast mast with ticketed observation decks and restaurants), and the neighbouring ridge the vast Çamlıca Mosque of 2019 — capacity 63,000, the largest in Asia Minor. What survives, and still earns the trip, is the summit park itself: Ottoman-styled tea houses, cafés and a restaurant run by the metropolitan municipality among monumental trees and flower gardens — the çay pavilions do still trade — and the panorama, which no construction has managed to block. What it is for: the dusk hour, when the city lights come up along the strait and the tea glasses steam. Go for the view; do not go for solitude. The tell — Dusk over the strait with a tulip glass of çay in the summit garden The catch — The summit is a destination for the whole city — weekends and holiday evenings are full. Tower decks are ticketed; we did not verify prices, and the hilltop itself costs nothing. Çamlıca, Üsküdar

landmarks|Büyük Valide Han.name: Büyük Valide Han
landmarks|Büyük Valide Han.teaser: The largest caravanserai in the city, still working — and no, you cannot go on the roof.
landmarks|Büyük Valide Han.body: Kösem Sultan — mother of two sultans, and for a stretch the most powerful woman in Ottoman history — built this around 1651 to fund her Çinili complex: 210 rooms around three courtyards, the largest historic han in Istanbul. It was the base of the city's Iranian merchant colony, whose small Shia mescit still stands in the courtyard; grand Muharram ceremonies were held here until 1927, when such processions were banned. It is severely dilapidated — the third courtyard is largely ruinous, with a Byzantine tower, the Tower of Eirene, standing at its corner — but it is not a ruin: a handful of foundry and mould-making workshops still trade in the galleries (most of the old textile ateliers have given way to wholesalers' storage), and that is the thing to see, a 17th-century building doing its original job. Now the truth the Instagram captions omit: the famous rooftop, with its dome-field view to the Golden Horn, was officially closed by the Culture and Tourism Ministry in 2016 after visitor traffic damaged the domes — warning signs are posted. Anyone offering to take you up for a banknote is selling you a violation of a closure order on a fragile roof. Go at working hours, walk the courtyards, and remember it is somebody's workplace. The tell — The main courtyard: workshops, the Iranian mescit, and the Byzantine tower behind The catch — Roof access banned since 2016 — we found no evidence of any legal reopening as of August 2026, and a fire broke out on that same roof in June 2026, so the fabric is more fragile than ever; check access on the day. Courtyards only, weekday working hours, and mind the crumbling stone. Mercan, Fatih — above the Grand Bazaar

landmarks|Rüstem Paşa Camii.name: Rüstem Paşa Camii
landmarks|Rüstem Paşa Camii.teaser: Sinan's tile box, hidden on a terrace above the market that pays for it.
landmarks|Rüstem Paşa Camii.body: You will walk past it unless you know: the mosque sits on a raised terrace above a block of vaulted shops in Tahtakale, and the way in is an easy-to-miss stair off the market street. The shops are not an accident — their rents endowed the mosque, commerce below, prayer above, which is the whole Ottoman city in one section drawing. Sinan finished it around 1563 for Rüstem Paşa, Süleyman's grand vizier and husband of Mihrimah Sultan, a man repairing his reputation with beauty. What makes it singular: some 2,300 İznik tiles in roughly eighty patterns cover the interior — no other mosque anywhere makes such lavish use of them — including the tomato-red Armenian bole, the pigment İznik's kilns mastered for a few decades in the 16th century and then lost forever. The red near the qibla wall is the colour ceramicists still cannot fully reproduce. Closed for years of restoration, it reopened for worship in 2021. Free; go between prayer times, dress covered, and give your eyes ten minutes to adjust. The tell — The lost İznik tomato-red on the qibla wall The catch — A working mosque — closed to visits during the five daily prayers, and shoulders and knees covered. Tahtakale, Eminönü — beside the Spice Bazaar · Working mosque — visit outside prayer times, free

landmarks|Küçük Ayasofya Camii.name: Küçük Ayasofya Camii
landmarks|Küçük Ayasofya Camii.teaser: Justinian's other Hagia Sophia — older ground, no queue, no ticket.
landmarks|Küçük Ayasofya Camii.body: Ten minutes downhill from the Sultanahmet queues stands the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, begun by Justinian early in his reign — scholars put it between 527 and 536, some arguing for the mid-520s, contemporary with the great Hagia Sophia and possibly earlier. It is the oldest surviving Justinianic church building in the city that you can simply walk into. The proof is carved into the building: around the interior runs the original Greek inscription frieze naming the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora — and, in a small act of sixth-century editing, mentioning Saint Sergius while leaving Saint Bacchus out. It became a mosque between 1506 and 1513 under Hüseyin Ağa, chief eunuch of the palace, was restored through 2006, and now works as a quiet neighbourhood mosque: octagon under a dome, whitewash and carved marble, carpet underfoot, mostly empty outside prayer times. What it is for: standing alone inside a sixth-century imperial building while the crowds queue up the hill. The tell — The marble frieze that still names Justinian and Theodora The catch — A working mosque — outside prayer times, shoes off, covered shoulders. The name on maps is Küçük Ayasofya Camii. Küçük Ayasofya, Fatih — below the Hippodrome · Working mosque — visit outside prayer times, free

landmarks|Şakirin Camii.name: Şakirin Camii
landmarks|Şakirin Camii.teaser: The mosque whose interior was designed by a woman — with the women's gallery given the best view in the room.
landmarks|Şakirin Camii.body: At an entrance to Karacaahmet, the great cemetery of the Asian side, stands the mosque the Şakir family built in memory of their own, opened on 7 May 2009. The architecture is Hüsrev Tayla's, but the reason to cross the water is the interior, by Zeynep Fadıllıoğlu — by the accounts around its opening, the first woman to design a mosque interior in modern Turkey. And it shows in one deliberate decision: the asymmetrical chandelier of waterdrop glass globes by Nahide Büyükkaymakçı — a prayer, the makers said, that light should fall on the congregation like rain — was hung so that the women's gallery, usually the worst seat in a mosque, has the clearest view of it. Add an acrylic minbar, dome calligraphy by Semih İrteş, and glass walls on three sides of the prayer hall, and you have the rare contemporary mosque that argues rather than imitates. A working mosque of about 500 places, free; go between prayers, and walk the old cemetery cypresses after. The tell — The rain-of-light chandelier, seen from the women's gallery The catch — A working mosque in a cemetery gate — quiet dress and quiet voice; visit outside prayer times. Karacaahmet, Üsküdar · Working mosque — visit outside prayer times, free

follow|Yemek ve Kültür.name: Yemek ve Kültür
follow|Yemek ve Kültür.teaser: The scholarly food journal that grew out of a Kadıköy kebab shop.
follow|Yemek ve Kültür.body: First issue January 2005 ; issue 84 is on the table now, four a year, print only, with no overseas subscription offered. Zeynep Dağdeviren is the responsible editor and Musa Dağdeviren sits on the board, filing seven forgotten folk recipes every issue. The advisory board carries Evangelia Balta , the historian of Turkish-speaking Ottoman Orthodox Christians — which tells you how seriously it takes the question of who actually cooked this food. yemekvekultur.com · Instagram @yemekvekulturdergisi_ciya · annual subscription delivers inside Turkey only

follow|Vedat Milor.name: Vedat Milor
follow|Vedat Milor.teaser: A Berkeley sociologist who became the country's most argued-with palate.
follow|Vedat Milor.body: Born 1955, schooled at Galatasaray Lisesi, economics at Boğaziçi, a masters at the LSE and a doctorate in sociology at Berkeley whose thesis the American Sociological Association named the best of 1990 . He turned that apparatus on restaurants, first in Milliyet and then in a long-running NTV programme, and edits the English-language Gastromondiale . In Istanbul his verdict moves a booking sheet the way a star does. gastromondiale.com in English · his social feeds and television work are Turkish

follow|Aylin Öney Tan.name: Aylin Öney Tan
follow|Aylin Öney Tan.teaser: The one Turkish food writer still filing weekly in English.
follow|Aylin Öney Tan.body: Her column runs in Hürriyet Daily News , Türkiye's oldest English-language daily, and it is current rather than archival — she was filing through July 2026. Recent pieces have covered gastronomic diplomacy at state dinners, the Culture Route Festival mapping fifty taste stops across Bursa, and the seasonal logic Istanbul kitchens actually work to. The best route into Anatolian regional food without a translator. hurriyetdailynews.com, opinion pages · free

follow|Oggusto and Gazete Oksijen.name: Oggusto and Gazete Oksijen
follow|Oggusto and Gazete Oksijen.teaser: Where the openings surface first, and why to read them with a raised eyebrow.
follow|Oggusto and Gazete Oksijen.body: Between them these two carry the city's rolling new-room lists, and they are usually ahead of the English-language listings. They are different animals. Oggusto is a luxury lifestyle and listings platform, with brand-partnered verticals and a shop sitting alongside the editorial. Gazete Oksijen is a general news weekly — Türkiye, world and economy desks, syndicated New York Times, Financial Times, Economist and Athletic copy — that also keeps a gastronomy section. Neither is a ranked guide. Treat everything as reported , not verified, and assume a share of the rooms will be gone within the year. oggusto.com and gazeteoksijen.com · Turkish only, free

follow|Culinary Backstreets.group: Written in English, reported on the ground
follow|Culinary Backstreets.name: Culinary Backstreets
follow|Culinary Backstreets.teaser: Two men in Istanbul writing up lunch, and they never lost the habit.
follow|Culinary Backstreets.body: It began as Istanbul Eats , a blog run by Ansel Mullins, who worked in historic restoration, and Yigal Schleifer, then the Christian Science Monitor 's Istanbul correspondent. The site first appears in the web archive in April 2009. It has since grown into food tours and reporting across close to thirty cities, but Istanbul remains the deepest desk, and istanbuleats.com now simply redirects here. culinarybackstreets.com — Istanbul city guide, daily dispatches, walking tours · free to read

follow|Cornucopia.group: Written in English, reported on the ground
follow|Cornucopia.name: Cornucopia
follow|Cornucopia.teaser: For people who came for the food and stayed for the Ottoman archive.
follow|Cornucopia.body: Launched in 1992 and made between Scotland, London and Turkey, it now runs two issues a year at a circulation above twenty thousand, edited by John Scott with Berrin Torolsan as publishing director. The register is connoisseurial — architecture, textiles, gardens, Anatolian archaeology — and it treats food as material culture rather than as a booking problem. The complete digital archive of every issue costs about nineteen pounds a year. cornucopia.net · print and digital · digital subscription around GBP 19 a year

follow|Turkey recap.group: Written in English, reported on the ground
follow|Turkey recap.name: Turkey recap
follow|Turkey recap.teaser: Why the bar you loved is suddenly not serving alcohol.
follow|Turkey recap.body: Independent and reader-supported, written by journalists based in Ankara and Istanbul; the flagship letter launched in 2019 and now runs politics and foreign affairs on Thursdays, business and economy on Fridays. Diego Cupolo co-founded it with Raziye Akkoç. Not a food publication — but licensing, alcohol regulation, inflation and the lira set what an Istanbul evening costs and whether the meyhane down the road can still pour. turkeyrecap.com · paid with a free trial · Turkish edition at studyorecap.com

follow|Ottoman History Podcast.name: Ottoman History Podcast
follow|Ottoman History Podcast.teaser: Academics talking properly, without the academic gate.
follow|Ottoman History Podcast.body: Started in March 2011 as an experiment in accessible scholarly production and became one of the largest digital resources of its kind on the Ottoman Empire and the modern Middle East. Chris Gratien, now at the University of Virginia, has recorded more than two hundred interviews. It carries no advertising and takes no revenue, and runs a parallel Turkish-language strand. Search the archive for coffee, wine, famine and the millet system. ottomanhistorypodcast.com · Apple Podcasts and Spotify · full episode guide online

follow|Salt Research.name: Salt Research
follow|Salt Research.teaser: An open archive inside the bank that financed the city it later lost.
follow|Salt Research.body: Salt's research library occupies the Alexandre Vallaury building on Bankalar Caddesi that once housed the Imperial Ottoman Bank, and it holds that bank's own archive along with collections on art, architecture and design, and city, society and economy. Much is digitised and searchable from anywhere. Walk out and the Camondo Stairs are a minute away, built in the 1870s by the Ottoman-Venetian Jewish banker Abraham Salomon Camondo. Salt Galata, Bankalar Caddesi 11, Karaköy 34421 · Tue-Sat 11.00-19.00 · free · archives at saltresearch.org

follow|İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Cu.group: What is actually on, the week you land
follow|İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Cu.name: İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts
follow|İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Cu.teaser: One foundation programmes most of the big weeks in the Istanbul year.
follow|İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Cu.body: It runs the Istanbul Film Festival, the Music Festival, the Jazz Festival, the Theatre Festival, the Istanbul Biennial and the Design Biennial, plus Filmekimi and the year-round Salon İKSV stage, and it curates the Turkish Pavilion at Venice. The calendar and the e-bulletin are the fastest way to learn whether your dates collide with something worth moving a dinner for. Both Turkish and English. iksv.org · calendar and e-bülten sign-up, free

follow|Argonotlar.group: What is actually on, the week you land
follow|Argonotlar.name: Argonotlar
follow|Argonotlar.teaser: The art press that covers the shows the institutions do not.
follow|Argonotlar.body: An independent, deliberately many-voiced contemporary-art platform that began publishing in 2020 , named after Maggie Nelson's The Argonauts . It runs criticism, interviews and argument rather than listings, and its ArgAjanda is a working diary of what is open across galleries and artist-run spaces. Turkish only. In a biennial year built around local initiatives, this is how you find out what those initiatives are actually doing. argonotlar.com · free Bülten newsletter and the ArgAjanda diary

follow|Bant Mag..group: What is actually on, the week you land
follow|Bant Mag..name: Bant Mag.
follow|Bant Mag..teaser: The continuous record of what independent has meant here since 2004.
follow|Bant Mag..body: First published in 2004 as a monthly print magazine called Bant , it now runs in print and online out of Istanbul across music, cinema, art and illustration, with an online issue archive, a radio and podcast strand, and an English section. The scene it has documented for two decades is the same one that fills the bars on Kadife Sokak — which makes it a listings source by accident. bantmag.com · Turkish with an English section · free

follow|Time Out Istanbul.group: What is actually on, the week you land
follow|Time Out Istanbul.name: Time Out Istanbul
follow|Time Out Istanbul.teaser: The English backstop when you need something open tonight.
follow|Time Out Istanbul.body: Time Out runs a full local Istanbul edition in both English and Türkçe, across restaurants and cafes, things to do, film, music and nightlife, art and culture. It is a commercial listings operation, not a critical guide, and it should never settle an argument about where to eat. For opening hours, one-off events and what has just appeared in the street you are standing in, it is the quickest English source. timeout.com/istanbul · free · English and Turkish editions
